Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a rate hike in December looks probable to him, and he did not rule out a bigger half-point move while price pressures remain stubborn. "While the precise timing of the hikes doesn't matter, ensuring that the promised hikes are implemented in a reasonable period of time does," Waller said, according to CNBC.

Traders see a quarter-point hike next month as all but certain, according to The Wall Street Journal. Waller's remarks pushed up Treasury yields.

Brent crude fell after President Donald Trump described renewed strikes on Iran as "quite unlikely."

In Europe, the pan-European Stoxx 600 was 0.6% higher. The U.K.’s FTSE 100 added 0.3%, France’s CAC 40 rose 0.9% and Germany’s DAX gained 0.9%.

In Asia, South Korea’s Kospi surged 4.3% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 added 2.9%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index rose 0.4%, mainland China’s CSI 300 added 0.3% and Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 gained 1.3%.

#5570. HECM endorsements rebound in October but stay near decade low

Federally insured reverse mortgage activity improved modestly in October 2026, with HECM endorsements rising 11% from September to 1,995, according to Reverse Market Insight and HECMWorld.com. The market remains near a 10-year low and slightly behind last year’s pace, with Finance of America, Longbridge and Mutual of Omaha dominating volume.   AI Summary

The federally insured reverse mortgage market posted a rebound in October, but activity remained at historically low levels compared to the past decade, according to data compiled by Reverse Market Insight (RMI) and published Friday by HECMWorld.com.

Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) endorsements rose to 1,995 in October, an 11% increase from September and the highest level in three months, the data shows. But even with the gain, this was the lowest figure for the month of October in at least 10 years.

Year to date, endorsements are about 3.19% below last year’s level — but comparisons are complicated by the federal government shutdown in October 2025, which disrupted activity and reporting.

Finance of America Reverse (FOA) remained the top HECM lender in October with 460 endorsements, followed by Longbridge Financial with 362 and Mutual of Omaha Mortgage with 332. Goodlife Home Loans posted 110 endorsements and Fairway Home Mortgage recorded 67.

Longbridge and Mutual of Omaha switched positions from September, and Goodlife jumped three spots by originating 62 more HECMs compared to the prior month. The top three lenders accounted for about 63% of all HECM endorsements in October, underscoring how concentrated the reverse mortgage business has become.

The number of active lenders with more than one HECM endorsement improved, rising to 75 in October from 63 in September.

From January through October, FOA widened its lead with 4,398 endorsements. Mutual of Omaha ranked second with 4,041, followed by Longbridge at 3,513, Goodlife at 916 and South River Mortgage at 692.

While endorsements increased, securitization volume moved in the opposite direction. HECM Mortgage-Backed Securities (HMBS) issuance in October was down 16% from September.

New View Advisors, citing its analysis of data from Ginnie Mae and private sources, reported that October HMBS issuance totaled $419 million, a decline of $27 million from September. There were 61 pools issued in October, nine fewer than in September.

FOA led all issuers in October with $180 million in HMBS issuance, up from $175 million in September. Longbridge and Mutual of Omaha saw month-over-month declines, issuing $116 million and $76 million, respectively.

First-participation pool production dropped to $238 million in October, down $28 million from September and $97 million from October 2025. New View said issuers “continue to struggle with the 10-year Treasury yield near 5%.”

From January to October, FOA was the top first-participation HMBS issuer with $1.01 billion of issuance, according to New View. Longbridge followed at $863 million and Mutual of Omaha at $593 million.

In October, the 61 HMBS pools consisted of 14 first-participation pools and 47 tail pools. New View also highlighted the ongoing use of very small pools as 18 of the October pools had an aggregate size below $1 million, totaling $10.8 million of unpaid principal balance that might not otherwise have been issued.

#5569. Meta introduces Muse Ember to power cost-efficient AI agents

Meta Platforms Inc. today introduced Muse Ember, an entry-level artificial intelligence model that costs significantly less than the competition.

Notably, it’s the first AI that the company trained using Muse Wonder. The latter algorithm is the Facebook parent’s flagship large language model. Meta didn’t specify which part of the workflow it automated with Muse Wonder.

One possibility is that the company used it to perform post-training, the task of honing a model’s capabilities by training it on additional data. Thinking Machines Labs Inc. recently demonstrated that even a relatively small LLM can run post-training runs end-to-end. Anthropic PBC, for its part, last week revealed that its AI models could soon gain the ability to significantly accelerate machine learning research.

Applications often use frontier LLMs such as Muse Wonder as part of AI ensembles. When a user enters a request, the frontier LLM splits it into smaller tasks and assigns them to agents powered by a lower-cost model. Meta says Muse Ember is specifically optimized to play the latter role.

The company evaluated the model using the Artificial Analysis Index, which aggregates nine AI benchmarks spanning use cases such as coding and financial analysis. Meta says that Muse Ember matched the score of Anthropic’s entry-level Claude Haiku 5.5 model at about a third the price. It also outperformed OpenAI Group PBC’s comparable GPT-6 Luna algorithm.

The same internal evaluation saw Meta test Muse Ember and the two rival models across nine other benchmarks. All three algorithms were in “max” mode, which means they used the maximum amount of hardware at their disposal instead of prioritizing cost-efficiency. Muse Ember outperformed Haiku and Luna across seven of the benchmarks.

The area where the model appears to have the biggest edge is business task automation. Whereas most of Muse Ember’s benchmark results were only a few percentage points better than those of Haiku and Luna, it clocked a 17% lead on AutomationBench-AA. It’s a collection of 657 tasks that span popular cloud applications such as Gmail and Salesforce.

Muse Ember has a context window of 1 million tokens, which enables it to ingest lengthy business documents. Users can also include images, audio and video in their prompts. The model generates responses up to 512,000 tokens in length.

Muse Ember is available through Meta’s Model API for 10 cents per million input tokens and 50 cents per million output tokens. A built-in cache can reuse frequently used prompts to avoid duplicate processing. When the feature is active, Muse Ember’s pricing drops to 0.4 cents per million input tokens.

Emirates anticipates receiving only three to five Boeing $BA 777-9 jets next year, and that is the optimistic scenario, President Tim Clark said at a press event in Berlin on Tuesday, according to Bloomberg.

Emirates has purchased more of the 777-9, a reworked take on Boeing's 777 widebody, than any other airline. The airline forecast only a small number of the jets arriving in late 2027, with perhaps double that volume to follow a year later, according to Bloomberg.

#5565. California voters reject measure to shred environmental red tape

California voters voted down Proposition 45, which sought to speed CEQA environmental reviews through standardized deadlines and faster court timelines. The measure lost 56% to 44% in unofficial returns, and the streamlining fight is expected to return to the Legislature.  AI Summary

California voters have rejected a ballot measure to speed environmental review of housing and other projects.

Proposition 45 would have consolidated a patchwork of legislative fixes to the California Environmental Quality Act, aimed largely at reducing a costly hurdle to building housing. The Associated Press called the race over the weekend, though the state is still counting votes. Unofficial returns showed about 56% of voters opposed and 44% in favor, a spread too large to overcome with the remaining votes.

It failed decisively across populous coastal counties, where housing affordability is a pressing concern. Voters in Santa Cruz, Marin and Sonoma counties rejected the measure by the widest margins.

Opponents tied the measure to data center development, an influential argument in midterm races nationwide.

“Californians have sent a clear message to corporate developers, utilities and data center builders that they will not stand for a broad assault at the ballot box on state law protecting our air, water and natural resources,” the Vote No on Prop 45 campaign released in a statement.

Proponents dubbed that an inaccurate scare tactic.

“The opposition relentlessly lied, falsely claiming that Prop 45 covered data centers when non-partisan experts agreed it did not – and used smokestack images and scare tactics about air and water pollution when the ‘essential projects’ included in Prop 45 did not include smokestack industries and also excluded mining, port, and other controversial projects,” Jennifer Hernandez, who leads Holland & Knight’s West Coast land-use and environmental group, told HousingWire TBD.

Opponents also countered the claim that the measure would help create affordable housing. They cited housing groups that urged a no vote or declined to endorse. Abundant Housing LA and California YIMBY, both of which endorsed L.A. Mayor-elect Nithya Raman, did not endorse the measure.

Opponents included the California Democratic Party, the League of Women Voters and the American Lung Association. Sierra Club California and the California Federation of Labor Unions also opposed it.

The California Chamber of Commerce sponsored the measure, with backing from home-builder groups and some affordable housing advocates.

“We were outspent but not outgunned, thanks to a broad bipartisan coalition that understood that Californians know we can have progress and safeguard our environment at the same time,” the campaign noted in its statement.

Had it passed, the measure would have capped full environmental impact reports at 365 business days. Court challenges would have faced a 270-day limit.

Covered “essential” projects included housing, water, energy, schools, health facilities and transportation. Applicants could have chosen the new procedures or the existing ones.

The Legislative Analyst’s Office said the measure could cost local governments up to $100 million a year at first. Long-term financial effects were unclear. A Chamber-commissioned analysis projected $1.5 billion in savings and added revenue over 10 years.

Prop. 45 followed a run of legislative changes that limited CEQA reviews of housing proposals. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 130 and Senate Bill 131 in 2025. They exempted qualifying infill housing from CEQA and narrowed review for some projects falling short of an exemption.

A newer round of bills signed this fall targets more permitting delays. Some shield specific developments from further CEQA challenges. One is a major mixed-use development in San Diego.

Backers argued those fixes helped only some projects. They said project-specific exemptions left other developments exposed to years of delay. Prop. 45 would have applied common deadlines to all eligible projects.

Supporters said predictable timelines would help California build homes and the infrastructure that serves them. They said CEQA lawsuits add tens of millions of dollars in costs, and thwart efforts to increase housing supply by escalating entitlement risk. They also argued that the measure could cut delays by two to 10 years.

“Not-in-my-backyard” and environmental groups have long sued local governments under CEQA. Those suits typically argue agencies did not properly handle environmental impact reviews.

A study by Hernandez and other researchers reviewed 498 CEQA appellate decisions from 2013 through 2023. Agencies prevailed in 75%. But the study said prolonged litigation still stalls financing and raises costs. It covers appellate decisions only and predates the 2025 reforms.

Opponents said the 2025 reforms already addressed much of CEQA’s housing problem. They said Prop. 45 would cap public-comment periods, narrow tribal consultation and limit judicial review. They also argued that affordability was being used as cover for a developer advantage.

Critics said “essential” was defined so broadly that it could fast-track freeways, power plants and pipelines.

The fight to streamline CEQA may now shift back to the Legislature and a new governor.

“We know this fight is not over,” the No on Prop 45 campaign wrote in its statement.

“The good news is that many millions of Californians voted for Prop 45, and do want timely, accountable, and predictable outcomes in CEQA,” Hernandez said. “Our legislative supporters saw the dirty trick campaign tactics unfold, and now have the opportunity to adopt these important CEQA reforms for the ‘essential projects’ that California needs to restore affordability to our state.”

#5563. Five FAQs homeowners have about private flood insurance

Private flood insurance is gaining attention as flooding shifts beyond mapped zones. Here are five common questions on coverage, NFIP differences, how private and NFIP policies can work together, eligibility and what homeowners policies typically exclude.   AI Summary

Extreme weather events caused by El Niño are dominating today’s headlines, driving an increased interest in flood insurance. However, flood patterns across the U.S. have been changing for years, even before El Niño. For example, catastrophic flooding is no longer dominated by events located in traditional flood zones or near coastal waters, but instead is increasingly defined by heavy rainfall.

As flood risks evolve, more homeowners are turning to private flood insurance – an alternative to coverage through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). For real estate agents guiding their clients through the home buying process, here is some basic information that clients need to know about this option.

Private flood insurance is a risk management tool backed by global capital markets that provides financial protection for buildings and personal property damaged by floods, helping families, communities and businesses to recover from these devastating events.

The primary difference between an NFIP and a private policy is the source of capital.

With an NFIP policy, FEMA holds all program risk, with United States taxpayers serving as the ultimate backstop. With private flood insurance, independent insurance companies bear the risk of loss. As a result, these companies leverage global capital structures to support risk selection and risk management in order to deliver a sustainable program capable of responding to customer needs.

While private insurers cannot be all things to all people, this disciplined and thoughtful approach means these insurers can deliver a sustainable and valuable product to their customers.

A private policy can act as either an alternative or a complement to an NFIP policy. Private policies equip agents with customizable options that can cater to individual homeowners’ needs, allowing insurance agents to craft solutions that ultimately help protect more people from floods.

Private policies can also complement an NFIP policy. If you have an NFIP policy, you can purchase private insurance to increase coverage beyond the limits offered by the federal program. Private insurance is also available to expand coverage, such as adding protection for contents in a basement or the expense to clean out a swimming pool.

The NFIP is essentially a one-size-fits-all policy available to almost every person in all geographies. However, the reality is that all homeowners aren’t the same. That’s the beauty of private insurance programs; they’re flexible programs that can respond to the individual needs of customers, like high-net-worth homeowners or renters.

Generally speaking, most homeowners’ policies exclude flood losses. A homeowners’ policy may cover water damage from broken pipes or sump pumps, but most exclude loss from inundation, whether resulting from swollen rivers, storm surge or intense rainfall.

The flood insurance industry is rapidly changing, and there are new opportunities coming online every day. To make the best decisions for clients, every real estate agent should take time to understand these new options.

In most situations, the home is the family’s most valuable investment. Wherever it rains, it can flood, so take time to consider solutions that can protect these treasured investments from catastrophe.

#5562. Infineon is raising its data center revenue forecast to nearly €4 billion

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The chipmaker forecasts fiscal 2027 revenue of about €20 billion, compared with €16.353 billion in fiscal 2026

Infineon raised its fiscal 2027 forecast for data center revenue to close to €4 billion ($4.5 billion) as it reported fourth-quarter results on Tuesday. The German chipmaker said revenue from power supplies for data centers is projected to reach that level in the year ending in September 2027.

Infineon forecast total revenue of roughly €20 billion ($22.4 billion) for fiscal 2027, up from the €16.353 billion it booked in fiscal 2026, assuming a EUR/USD exchange rate of 1.15. The company expects a segment result margin in the mid-20s percent band, up from the 19.7% it recorded for fiscal 2026.

Infineon's earlier forecast covered AI data center power solutions only, at €2.5 billion, according to Bloomberg. The new figure combines those solutions with traditional data centers, which generate about €500 million a year.

JPMorgan $JPM analysts had expected fiscal 2027 data center revenue of between €3.5 billion and €4 billion, according to Bloomberg.

"Supported by an ongoing cyclical recovery and strong demand in our structural growth areas, we expect a significant increase in revenue and profitability in fiscal year 2027," CEO Jochen Hanebeck said in a statement. He cited electromobility, software-defined vehicles, energy infrastructure and semiconductor solutions for data center power supplies as key contributors.

Fourth-quarter revenue was €4.706 billion, with a segment result of €1.119 billion and a margin of 23.8%. Fiscal 2026 revenue rose 12% from a year earlier. For the first quarter of fiscal 2027, Infineon expects revenue of about €4.6 billion and a segment result margin of about 23%.

For fiscal 2027, the company is guiding to an adjusted gross margin between the mid- and high-40s in percentage terms, and it has earmarked €3.0 billion to €3.5 billion for investment. It forecast adjusted free cash flow of about €2.2 billion and free cash flow of about €1.8 billion.

The main investment areas are production equipment at the Dresden facility in Germany, capacity for silicon carbide in Malaysia and gallium nitride output using 300-millimeter wafers in Villach, Austria, according to Bloomberg.

Infineon's management board intends to propose a dividend of €0.38 a share, up €0.03, at the annual general meeting in February 2027. Infineon stock rose 3.3% to €50.23 in Frankfurt trading on Tuesday morning.

#5561. PitchBook opens its platform to startups for free and debuts Origin deal sourcing service

Private markets data provider PitchBook Data Inc. today opened its platform to startups for free at Web Summit in Lisbon.

Those that sign up have to share their financials. Some of that information will reach investors through the company’s new deal sourcing service, PitchBook Origin.

The launches come as more startups than ever are landing a first round. In the U.S., the 2021 record for first-time financings had already fallen by the end of September, PitchBook and the National Venture Capital Association found in their latest Venture Monitor report.

PitchBook credits artificial intelligence with part of that growth, since the technology has made companies easier to start. AI tools have also compressed investor diligence from weeks to days. Sourcing has not kept pace, the company argues, particularly where the signals are not public.

Free access for startups runs through a program called PitchBook for Startups. Founders who have bootstrapped or raised only from angels, grants or accelerators qualify as long as they are now seeking a first institutional round and can show at least a mockup of their product.

Once a startup has handed over its financials and details on its leadership team and product, its founders can use the PitchBook platform to research which firms are actively writing checks in their sector and stage. Investor research tops PitchBook’s own list of what founders can do with the access.

That founder data lands in a much bigger pool on the Origin side, where coverage starts at about 25 million companies and 250 million people profiles. Bootstrapped businesses and companies that have not yet raised money or announced what they are building are part of that count, and some 15 million of the companies are new to PitchBook.

Third-party data enrichment and PitchBook’s own machine learning models supply part of the coverage. PitchBook said it has not had founder-verified data at scale before.

Each company gets a score, and investors can tune relevance filters to their own criteria. Real-time alerts, saved searches and customer relationship management integrations are meant to replace the manual monitoring that deal teams do now.

Chief Solutions Officer Paul Santarelli said the missing piece for investors has been visibility into “the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see.” Every company that joins the startup program and contributes verified information sharpens that picture, he said.

PitchBook “was once a startup itself, working to get in front of the right backers,” President and Chief Operating Officer Rod Diefendorf said. Founded in 2007, the Seattle company now serves more than 100,000 clients worldwide. Morningstar Inc. has owned it since 2016.

Startups can apply for the program now. Origin is available as a standalone product or as an add-on to the main PitchBook platform.

#5559. AI is already in real estate, and its next opportunity is connection

Surveys show broad AI use across real estate and title. The next opportunity is connecting data across systems so teams can answer file status, reduce re-entry and route tasks with clear review and permissions.  AI Summary

In real estate, a simple customer question can send a professional searching across several systems: “Where is my file?” AI’s next opportunity is to help bring the answer into view.

Imagine being able to answer that question with the relevant information already in view. The order, the outstanding requirements and the next steps would be available to the person helping the customer. That is an exciting prospect for an industry where getting an answer can still mean checking several systems and making a few calls.

For real estate and title, AI becomes more useful when it can reach the information people need to do their jobs.

We already have momentum. In a Realtors Property Resource survey of 225 real estate professionals, 82% of respondents said they use AI in their business, commonly for listing descriptions and emails. Qualia’s 2025 survey of 631 title and escrow professionals found that nearly 90% of respondents use at least one AI tool.

People are putting AI to work. Now we have an opportunity to connect that work across the transaction.

A connected workflow could draw on information from across the transaction. Think about what that could mean for a title professional answering a customer, an underwriter reviewing a file or a manager deciding where a team needs help.

Of course, real estate has its own complications. A title file depends on agents, lenders, underwriters, public records and production systems. Requirements vary locally. Acquisitions bring together companies with different technology and processes. Connecting that environment takes work, but the benefits show up in very practical places.

Start with a field conversation. Relationships drive this business, and representatives learn valuable information while talking with agents and referral partners. Capturing activity from a phone while it is fresh could help teams schedule follow-ups and give colleagues a shared view.

Picture that information reaching the appropriate team while the conversation is still recent. The follow-up begins with context. Colleagues know what was discussed and can help move it forward. A customer benefits from the relationship without having to start the conversation over with each new person.

Then look at intake. Purchase agreement terms arrive in a document, but they need to become information the production team can use. A connected workflow could extract those terms for a person to verify against the source agreement before transferring the approved information into production. That could reduce repeated entry and help carry consistent information into the next stage of the file.

For the employee, that could mean less time retyping details. For the customer asking about progress, connecting customer and order information could make it easier to provide a dependable answer.

Title review offers another useful example. An examiner identifies a commitment requirement. Connecting that finding to a trackable task in production, with examiner sign-off, could give the work a clear next step. The team could see what needs attention and track it through resolution.

These are the kinds of improvements worth getting excited about. They put better information within reach and help professionals spend more time serving customers and moving transactions forward.

Title professionals know that an answer is only useful if they can trust it. Connecting information should make its source easier to see and professional review easier to perform.

Legal description and survey checks are also areas to explore, including flagging potential discrepancies in property boundary measurements. Automation could help direct a professional’s attention to an issue that needs investigation, with qualified review determining its significance.

The same principle applies when an output affects a document or recorded instrument. Keep the source visible, establish the appropriate review and record the final decision. AI can help organize information and flag issues, while qualified professionals remain responsible for title-related judgments and approvals. In title, accuracy is the product.

Permissions belong in the workflow from the beginning, too. Decide what a tool can access, which actions it can take and when human review or approval is required. Log its actions so the team can understand how a result was reached. Those decisions help make connected workflows dependable enough for people to use with confidence.

For leaders deciding where to begin, I would start by following a single file through its handoffs. Where do people re-enter information? Where does a finding wait for someone to assign the next action? Which customer questions take several conversations to answer?

Choose one connection to improve, then measure the difference. Look at repeated entry, response times and whether customers receive clearer answers. Let those results guide the next step.

We have experienced professionals, valuable information and people already willing to work with AI. Bringing those strengths together can help make each handoff more useful and each customer conversation more informed. That is progress customers will feel. And that is worth building.

Ryan Ozonian is the Senior Director of Innovation & AI at Williston Financial Group.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5558. Polymarket's annualized revenue has topped $1.8 billion

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The prediction market's annual revenue run rate was above $1 billion in June, after it opened its U.S. exchange

Thomas Fuller / SOPA Images / LightRocket / Getty Images

Polymarket told CNBC on Tuesday that its annualized revenue has surpassed $1.8 billion, up from a run rate above $1 billion in June.

The growth is coming from Polymarket's U.S. exchange, a standalone marketplace that runs independently of the company's international DeFi platform, according to CNBC. In October, the domestic exchange processed notional volume of more than $14.5 billion, compared with $4 billion in June, according to CNBC, which cited TickerTracker data.

CNBC credited the jump in volume to high-traffic events such as the summer's FIFA World Cup and the NFL season kickoff in September. Combo event contracts, which operate much like sportsbook parlays that bundle several legs together, made up over 70% of the platform's trading activity on Sunday, according to CNBC.

Polymarket has started raising $1 billion in new funding, a round that puts its valuation at $21 billion, according to CNBC.

Polymarket had said in June that its annualized revenue had surpassed $1 billion, six weeks after its U.S. exchange opened to the public. Access widened in mid-May when the company removed the waitlist for mobile app users. The U.S. exchange had been in a restricted period since its December debut.

The company faces regulatory and political questions, according to CNBC. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is running a wide-ranging investigation of Polymarket, examining its advertising practices and whether it breached an earlier settlement requiring it to keep U.S. residents off its international exchange.

Polymarket could also draw heavier scrutiny under a Democratic Congress, in part because Donald Trump Jr., the son of President Donald Trump, advises the company, according to CNBC.

A Polymarket spokesperson told CNBC the company intends to cooperate with legislators while they get up to speed on the prediction market industry. "We welcome scrutiny," the spokesperson said.

#5557. Why homebuilders need business plans that test scenarios

Scott Cox explains why forcing long-range plans to match annual budgets shifts focus to deadlines over analysis. He recommends a 1-page output and a scenario-ready model leaders can adjust without analyst help.  AI Summary

[In the fourth of seven excerpts from ‘Less Wrong, More Right,’ Scott Cox argues argues a 5-year business plan should be a thinking tool, not a control document. He shares two tests: keep key output to one page and use a single assumptions page for scenario changes.]

Sometimes I think the most misunderstood part of our business is the business plan.

The real purpose is to learn about your business and understand the consequences of the choices available to you. If we go in this direction, what does it mean for our capitalization and our risk? How many people will we need, and when? Is our subcontractor base capable of that volume? For this to pay off, how long does the market have to hold? A plan exists to force that thinking. Everything else it does — satisfying the bank, setting the bonus targets, giving the board something to approve — is a byproduct, and the byproducts have a way of eating the main course.

I sat in a business plan meeting for the division of a multi-region builder. A number of organizational things were in flux, the market was slipping, and to be fair to the local team, they were being asked to work on too many initiatives at once. While everyone debated next year’s goals, I was looking at year five. I did a simple return-on-assets calculation on the page in front of me. It was terrible. I asked whether that was really what they expected, because if that was the plan, I could not support doing any new deals at all. The return on capital did not justify the investment.

After what I will politely describe as an agitated discussion, we got down to the why — the size of the deals, the type of deals, the organizational structure, the capital those choices required. And that should have become the start of a worthwhile conversation. Next year’s results were, within limits, going to be what they were going to be. The bigger issues were the ones worth the room’s time.

Then the deadline arrived. Divisional plans had to be consolidated. The banks and others were waiting. Some minor tweaks were made and the plan went out substantially as drafted. I doubt anyone looked past year one in that document ever again.

That is the failure I want to dwell on, because it was not a failure of intelligence or effort. It was a process that answered to form and deadline instead of thought — a date to hit, a box to check — and once those became the real assignment, the thinking we’d just started in that room stopped mattering.

What we should have been able to do, right there, was stop the meeting and start putting different approaches into the model. Bigger deals, fewer of them. Entitled land versus unentitled. Different timing. Then look at what came out — capital required, when it came back, what the returns actually were. We could not, so we did not. The model was capable of producing one future in enormous detail and incapable of producing a second one at all.

Underneath all of this is an instinct I want to focus on, because it is the one doing the damage. People believe everything should foot. The five-year plan should tie to the annual budget, which should tie to the phase budgets, which should tie to the cash flow. It feels like discipline. It is not.

Budgets are control instruments. Plans are thinking instruments. A control instrument has to foot — that is its job. A six-month cash flow projection cannot be materially wrong without serious consequences. An annual budget is an accountability document and people are going to be held to it. A phase budget for a project you are about to start is a commitment on money you are about to spend. All of those demand precision.

A five-year company plan does not. It is for asking what happens if we run this business differently? When you force a thinking instrument to reconcile with a control instrument, the thinking instrument always loses — because the deadline always belongs to the control instrument. That is not a hypothetical. That is exactly what happened in the meeting I just described.

The first is the one-page test, and it is a test of the output. If what you circulate, at least the important parts, does not fit on an 11×17, you have included things that do not matter. That is partly a communication discipline — that is how a lot of people are actually going to read it — but it is mostly a forcing function. Something has to be left off, and deciding what gets left off is the same as deciding what matters.

The second is a test of the design of the model, and it is the one I care about more. Can the CEO change the assumptions herself, in the room, in real time, to test an idea — without the analyst who built the model sitting next to her? Can I take it home, pour a bourbon after dinner, and try three scenarios on my own? If the answer is yes, the model is simple enough. If the answer is no, you do not have a tool. You have a document.

Back-up tabs are fine. Detail underneath is fine. The requirement is that a single, clearly marked assumptions page drives all of it with comprehensible results, and that changing one thing changes everything downstream without anyone opening the hood.

The principle underneath is that granularity should be set by what you need to move, not by what the budget happens to contain.

The 11×17 should just be a bigger, prettier version of the yellow pad. If it is anything more than that, ask yourself what all the rest of it is actually for.

Adapted from Less Wrong, More Right (Part III: Running the Business), available on Amazon.

#5555. Blackstone will buy a 15.57% stake in Indian lender IIFL Finance for about $532 million

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The investment is expected to lift IIFL's capital adequacy ratio to about 30% from roughly 17% on a pro forma basis as of September

Blackstone is set to buy 15.57% of Indian shadow lender IIFL Finance in a deal worth roughly 50 billion rupees ($532 million), according to Bloomberg.

The investment will be routed via Singapore-based Ingot SG Pte. Ltd., which is set to take roughly 83.1 million preference shares that are compulsorily convertible, priced at 602 rupees each, according to Bloomberg. Every preference share will convert into IIFL Finance equity at a one-for-one ratio.

IIFL Finance stock ended Monday's session at 627 rupees, roughly 4% over Blackstone's entry price. The stock is up roughly 3% so far in the current year.

Under the fundraising, IIFL founder Nirmal Jain will take up 15 million warrants valued at 9.03 billion rupees, according to Bloomberg. Co-founder R. Venkataraman will take up 4.5 million warrants, valued at 2.71 billion rupees. Ardent Impex Private Ltd., an entity of the founder group, will take 1.5 million warrants valued at 903 million rupees.

Jain and Mukesh Mehta, chief investment officer of Blackstone India Private Equity, said in a statement the deal will shore up the lender's finances and back its growth, according to Bloomberg. The expansion includes technology spending as well as co-lending tie-ups with banks. Blackstone said it intends to partner with IIFL's management team as the lender keeps expanding.

On a pro forma basis as of September, the capital infusion is expected to raise IIFL Finance's capital adequacy ratio from roughly 17% to about 30%, according to Bloomberg.

Bloomberg News reported back in September that Blackstone was one of several international investors weighing a stake in IIFL Finance. Fairfax Financial Holdings bought a 60.72% holding in IDBI Bank in October, paying 528.78 billion rupees, according to Bloomberg; as of the end of September, it owned about 13.6% of IIFL Finance.

Blackstone committed roughly 62 billion rupees last year in return for a stake of up to 9.99% in Federal Bank, according to Bloomberg. The firm also controls mortgage lender Aadhar Housing Finance.

IIFL Finance lends against gold and provides home loans, business loans, property-backed financing and credit for small and medium-sized enterprises. The lender runs upward of 4,900 branches spanning more than 500 Indian cities and manages roughly 1.15 trillion rupees in assets, according to Bloomberg.

#5554. AI security startup Bay launches with $50M to vet agent actions before they run

Israeli artificial intelligence security startup Bay AI Inc. launched today with $50 million in funding to let enterprises vet each action an AI agent tries to take before it runs.

Bay provides software that tracks the agents working across a company, whether they sit on an employee’s laptop, inside a cloud workload or in a software-as-a-service application. One set of policies covers them all.

First-generation AI security tools mostly filter prompts and responses. Bay argues that misses where the damage happens, since a harmless-looking prompt can still end with an agent deleting a production database.

The founders ran into that kind of failure themselves when one of their own coding agents, working with its normal permissions, tried to expose a cloud environment to the internet to finish a test. They still have the screenshot.

Bay installs through the mobile device management or endpoint detection and response tools a customer already has, and the company says it takes under five minutes. A scanner called Wave inventories the agents, extensions and local models on each machine and leaves nothing running once it finishes.

Each time an agent proposes an action, the AI tool running it hands the request to Bay Enforcer, a static binary, through a native hook. The check happens on the machine itself with the whole session as context, and Bay said a verdict comes back in milliseconds, sometimes as a prompt asking the user to approve the step. Anything judged too risky never runs.

The policy behind those verdicts comes from Bay’s Lighthouse system, which drafts a separate one for each team from the last 30 days of agent activity, so security staff are not writing rules every time someone picks up a new tool. Teams can test a policy against the previous month first and see what it would have stopped. Bay said false positives run under 1%.

Security leaders are often handed an enterprise-wide AI rollout with a year-end deadline, co-founder and Chief Executive Yuval Zacharia said, or find that agents have already spread across the company and “it’s the Wild West.” She wants security to become “the reason AI ships faster, not the reason it stalls.”

Micron Technology Inc., Wix.com Ltd., ClickUp Inc. and Peloton Interactive Inc. are among the dozens of enterprise customers signed in the nine months since Bay was founded. Fortune 100 companies on the platform tripled their use of autonomous agents in just under 30 days, the company said.

Zacharia founded Bay with Chief Product Officer Aner Morag and Vice President of Research and Development Boris Danilovich. The three knew each other from the Israel Defense Forces’ Unit 8200, where Zacharia led a department of about 50 people before becoming the first intelligence officer there to cross into offensive cyber operations. After the military she ran security research and AI at Cyber Hunters Ltd.

Danilovich was an early employee at Preempt Security Inc. and stayed six years at CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. after it bought the startup in 2020. Most of Bay’s research team followed him over. Morag was the first employee at Noname Security.

The $50 million comes from two rounds. Battery Ventures LP led the larger $37 million Series A round, and Micron’s venture arm, Micron Ventures, also participated after the chipmaker started out as a Bay customer. Wiz Inc. Chief Executive Assaf Rappaport put in money personally. The remaining $13 million came from a previously undisclosed seed round co-led by YL Ventures Ltd. and Striker Venture Partners.

Yoav Leitersdorf, managing partner at YL Ventures, said his firm looked at a crowded field of AI endpoint security companies before picking Bay. He believes it can become “as fundamental to enterprise AI adoption as the network firewall was to the internet era.”

Engineering and product hiring will continue in Tel Aviv, where Bay is based, with the sales, marketing and customer teams growing in the U.S. and Europe. Enterprises can buy the platform now.

#5553. Asset Based Lending closes $200M securitization

Asset Based Lending closed its largest deal, a $200M unrated securitization backed by business-purpose residential loans. ABL 2026 RTL-1 allows up to 65% ground-up infill construction collateral and brings cumulative securitization volume to $723M.  AI Summary

Asset Based Lending (ABL), a private real estate lender, announced on Tuesday that it closed a $200 million securitization, its largest to date, backed by business-purpose residential real estate loans, including a significant concentration of ground-up construction loans.

The transaction, ABL 2026 RTL-1, priced Oct. 15 and closed Oct. 26. It marks the company’s fourth unrated securitization and brings its cumulative securitization volume to $723 million.

Up to 65% of the collateral pool is eligible to consist of ground-up infill construction loans, a segment that has been central to ABL’s lending strategy since 2014.

The transaction came amid volatility in the securitization market and increased investor scrutiny of credit risk, said Daniel Gotay, ABL’s head of capital markets. Despite these conditions, the company secured what he described as some of the tightest pricing levels for an unrated issuer.

“What is most exciting about this one is that we’re not just doing our fourth, but that the market was a tricky market this time around,” Gotay said in an interview with HousingWire. “For us to execute at one of the sharpest levels for an unrated issuer, and to do that with the highest concentration of ground-up construction, really spoke to the presence that we’ve worked hard to build on Wall Street.”

Gotay said investors were particularly focused on how lenders would manage credit and construction risks over the next two years. ABL completed more than 20 virtual investor meetings ahead of the transaction, highlighting its underwriting and servicing practices.

The company services its loans in-house and uses a high-touch approach to managing projects, Gotay said. He added that investors also evaluated ABL’s broader portfolio, which has maintained a weighted average credit score of 740 and a weighted average loan-to-value ratio of 64%.

ABL has kept its weighted average LTV in the low 60% range for much of the past decade, Gotay said, contrasting that with some competing securitizations featuring LTV ratios in the upper-60% to low-70% range.

Investor appetite for the asset class remains strong despite heightened caution, Gotay said. International capital, including funds based in the United Kingdom and Japan, is increasingly looking to invest in U.S. asset-backed securities. “Even though they’re a little more on guard because of what’s happening, they still have to deploy their money for this type of asset,” he said.

Kevin Rodman, CEO of Asset Based Lending, said the transaction reflects the company’s experience in financing residential construction.

“We are proud to lead the industry in financing ground-up construction, and to do it at a cost that keeps our pricing competitive for the builders we serve,” Rodman said in a statement. “This transaction underscores the strength of the platform our team has built and the confidence investors have in our credit. Every one of these loans puts new housing on the ground.”

Gotay said ground-up construction has long been a core part of ABL’s business and will remain a significant share of its lending activity.

“The firm is really built to manufacture and manage infill ground-up construction since, really, 2014,” he said. “That’s been our specialty in the market and where we win the most deals.”

Performance Trust Capital Partners served as structuring agent, while Nomura Securities International and Mizuho Securities USA served as joint bookrunners.

The securitization also reflects ABL’s expanding geographic footprint, with collateral spanning the Northeast, Sun Belt, Rust Belt and South. The company said it plans to grow beyond its established Northeast presence and finance residential development in additional markets across the country.

#5551. Trump says Iran war could end "fairly soon" after Qatar talks, plays down new strikes

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Oil prices slid on Tuesday as the president called new U.S. strikes on Iran "quite unlikely," though Iran disputes that talks are under way

President Donald Trump said on Monday the conflict with Iran might end "fairly soon," following his White House meeting with Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani.

"We're seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it's going to be ending fairly soon," Trump told reporters. He said Tehran was "talking very politely" with Washington.

Trump described new U.S. strikes on Iran as "quite unlikely," though he said the U.S. could resume them if circumstances change. He repeated that Tehran will never be permitted to obtain nuclear arms.

In a Truth Social post, Trump said Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait "prefer the status quo," which includes the naval blockade of Iran, according to CNBC.

Al Thani said he was "grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region," according to Bloomberg. Bloomberg, citing an unnamed official, said negotiations are expected to continue and military escalation is unlikely while they do.

Large gaps remain. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Sunday that the talks "hadn't been very productive" because of Iranian demands, according to Bloomberg. Tehran is demanding that the U.S. end its blockade of Iranian Persian Gulf ports and drop sanctions before any negotiations begin. Washington wants Iran to halt its strikes on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz and to give ground on its nuclear work.

Iran has sent the U.S. a proposal through Qatari intermediaries under which the Strait of Hormuz could reopen within two days, in exchange for sanctions relief and a different shipping lane through the strait, according to CNBC. Washington was reviewing it, CNBC said. Iranian officials dispute that talks are under way. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Washington should stop “manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks,” according to CNBC.

Oil prices fell after Trump suggested the conflict might wrap up soon. Brent crude for January delivery was down 2.7% at $90.14 at 5:33 a.m. ET on Tuesday, a level not seen since August. U.S. West Texas Intermediate was down 2.4% at $84.78.

The U.S. and Israel began the war with strikes on Iran. A truce followed in early April, and the two sides agreed in mid-June to a memorandum of understanding that included a ceasefire. It collapsed about two weeks later, according to Bloomberg.

Republicans lost both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, according to Bloomberg, and Vice President JD Vance named the war as the main reason.

#5549. Why Is Crypto Down? Jensen Huang Chinese Spy Scandal Sends AI Stocks Into Chaos

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

We’re back to the same question again: Why is crypto down? Bitcoin and altcoins are taking another beating as Wall Street’s AI trade starts unraveling. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is now at the center of a growing Chinese espionage scandal. His alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset has put the world’s most valuable chipmaker under fresh scrutiny.

The timing could hardly be worse for investors. Technology stocks have already suffered a brutal selloff, with the Nasdaq entering correction territory. Nvidia shares plunged 9.3% during Thursday’s rout, while semiconductor stocks suffered their worst session in years.

NEW: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits to cheating on his wife two days after a report dropped that U.S. intelligence believes he had a relationship with a Chinese spy."I was unfaithful to my wife," Huang said in a letter to Nvidia staff."My actions hurt her and our children.… pic.twitter.com/moB9B3nYlI

Now, an investigation into Huang’s personal and professional connections could introduce another shock. If confidence in Nvidia starts cracking, the consequences could extend well beyond the AI industry. Bitcoin and the wider crypto market are already feeling the pressure.

The latest crypto selloff follows a dramatic reversal across US technology markets. Bitcoin erased its post-election rally, falling below $75,000. Ethereum dropped more than 7%, while XRP and Solana also suffered heavy losses.

The Nasdaq Composite plunged 5.5% during the same session. The Nasdaq 100 lost 6.4%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index crashed 12%. Nvidia and AMD were among the biggest casualties.

This selloff has been DEVASTATING.The AI stocks have erased $13.2 TRILLION in market value from stocks’ 2026 highs.Only U.S and China have an annual GDP larger than that loss.Market value erased at six AI giants:– Alphabet: $1.62 trillion lost (−32%)– Nvidia: $1.49… pic.twitter.com/i065m2W4b4

More than $2.5 trillion in Nasdaq market cap disappeared during October. Investors are increasingly questioning if massive AI infrastructure investments will deliver sufficient returns. Major technology companies continue pouring billions into chips, data centers, and computing infrastructure.

Then add political uncertainty, which is adding another headache. Democrats secured control of both congressional chambers during the US midterm elections. Investors now fear greater opposition to data center expansion and potentially tougher regulatory scrutiny.

The resulting selloff has exposed how closely crypto trades with speculative technology investments. Bitcoin increasingly moves alongside high-growth equities when institutional investors adjust their risk exposure.

The damage has also spread into derivatives markets. More than $1 billion in leveraged crypto positions disappeared during Thursday’s selloff. Most liquidations involved traders betting on higher prices.

That forced selling can quickly turn an ordinary correction into something considerably uglier. As Bitcoin falls, liquidations push prices lower and expose leveraged altcoin positions to further losses.

Nvidia’s problems have suddenly become considerably more personal. The company’s board announced an independent investigation yesterday. It wants to examine reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

The controversy involves Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. US authorities reportedly suspected her of being a Chinese intelligence asset.

Megaspeed has also faced scrutiny over allegations involving access to advanced Nvidia chips restricted from export to China. Republican lawmakers have requested a briefing from Huang regarding the allegations.

Separately, Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife. He apologized to his family and colleagues, accepting responsibility for his actions.

BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, CEO Jensen Huang sends a company-wide email regarding his recently reported relationship with a Chinese spy. pic.twitter.com/NTdoSgaxoy

The combination creates an uncomfortable situation for Nvidia shareholders. Huang is not simply another corporate executive. He remains the public face of the AI revolution and one of its most influential decision-makers.

A prolonged investigation could introduce uncertainty around Nvidia’s leadership, relationships with international customers, and exposure to geopolitical tensions.

Nvidia’s board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. However, the investigation could keep the controversy alive while investors are already questioning AI valuations.

The biggest concern for crypto is what happens if the AI selloff spreads. Nvidia has become a central pillar of the global technology investment cycle. Its chips power the infrastructure behind many of the world’s largest AI projects.

If investors begin questioning the sustainability of that investment cycle, semiconductor stocks, data center operators, and technology companies could face another round of selling.

Bitcoin is particularly exposed because institutional investors increasingly treat it as part of their risk portfolios. When confidence disappears from technology markets, crypto often loses buyers alongside speculative equities.

The Binance security incident has added another source of pressure. The exchange’s clients withdrew approximately $6.1 billion following the exchange’s recent security breach.

That creates an uncomfortable combination of falling institutional confidence, weaker market liquidity, and leveraged positions being forced out. Bitcoin now needs a recovery in risk appetite to regain momentum. Otherwise, another wave of technology stock selling could drag crypto prices lower.

So why is crypto down? The AI market has a new problem to deal with, and Bitcoin is discovering that Nvidia’s troubles can become its troubles too.

#5547. Teleport makes Beams generally available to bring AI agents into production

Infrastructure identity company Teleport today made Teleport Beams, its runtime for artificial intelligence agents that work on production infrastructure, generally available.

Beams goes after what Teleport sees as the main reason agents have stayed out of production so far. Most enterprises have not plugged agents into those systems at all, according to Ev Kontsevoy, Teleport’s co-founder and chief executive. He blamed gaps such as delegated identity and an audit trail that follows an agent from intent to action.

Sandboxes, the tool many teams reach for now, mostly isolate the agent in a virtual machine and handle its credentials. “When the cost of an error is high, traditional sandboxes don’t cut it,” Kontsevoy said ahead of the announcement.

Teleport calls each individual runtime a Beam, and every agent gets its own. A Beam carries a delegated identity inherited from the user or agent that launched it, while the agent inside starts with no standing privileges. Work begins with a proposed execution plan. That plan can be revised by a person or by a large language model acting as judge before a separate Beam runs it with only the approved roles. Reviewers then see new requests only for steps outside the plan.

Passwords never enter the agent’s environment. Everything the agent sends to a model is traced, and Teleport says that record lets Beams pick out a hijacked goal or agents coordinating in ways nobody planned. Each session also gets scored against the MITRE ATT&CK framework for a written risk summary. Seven of the detection rules come prebuilt, privilege escalation among them. Anything else a customer wants caught can be described in natural language and added to the set.

Each Beam is an ephemeral micro-VM on a virtualized network. Nothing gets in or out without passing Teleport’s controls, and the audit log keeps a copy of every protocol exchange. Snapshots taken by a feature named Phases carry the files and memory of an expiring Beam into the next one, so longer jobs do not have to start over.

Teams can also fork a Beam to try several approaches in parallel. When something goes badly wrong, a kill switch ends the agent’s activity and cuts all of its connections to production at once.

Teleport makes no promise about what a model will decide. A hijacked or mistaken agent inside a Beam can reach only what it was granted until its authority lapses at the end of the task, and every action it takes stays on the record.

Beams runs on top of the Teleport Infrastructure Identity Platform, which the company says is in production at more than 700 enterprises, Nasdaq Inc., DoorDash Inc. and Elastic N.V. among them. Cisco Systems Inc. became Teleport’s largest strategic investor in August.

Teleport first showed Beams in March, two months after publishing the Teleport Agentic Identity Framework that the runtime now puts into practice. Following a public beta, the product is available at beams.run.

#5546. AI promised 10x. Most companies got 1.2x. Wrike founder Andrew Filev launches Hops to close the gap

AI made people faster. Hops is built to make teams faster.

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Hopsâ¢ Collaborative AI workspace opens to everyone today, after more than 2,500 teams used it in early access. Until now, AI at work has mostly meant individuals working out of their own private chat windows. Built by Wrike founder Andrew Filev, Hops brings AI to teamwork: people and AI work together in everything from chats and docs to slides and custom apps, and what one person teaches Hops, the whole team can use.

AI can now do in minutes what used to take an afternoon. But businesses don't run on one-off deliverables. They run on projects and programs that whole teams move forward together. Most AI tools are still built for one person in a private chat with an assistant such as ChatGPTâ¢. Teammates copy and paste results, repeat context and coordinate next steps by hand, and what each person learns stays buried in their own chats. Individuals got faster. Their companies barely did.

"I spent 20 years building software to help teams work together. Then AI arrived, and the industry started building tools for people to work alone," said Filev, founder and CEO of Hops. "When I ask founders and executives of established companies how much faster their company moves than it did a year ago, the answer is usually 10 to 20 percent. That's well short of 2x, and of what the individual gains would suggest. The PC era didn't pay off when PCs got faster. It paid off when they were networked. I believe AI will follow the same path."

Adding an AI bot to an existing collaboration tool only takes a team so far. That's why the Hops team built the whole workspace from the ground up, so AI works inside everything a team uses, down to its own custom apps.

On the Hops team, every ad, email and landing page used to wait in line for the head of marketing's review. Then she taught Hops the marketing voice: which message leads, what each audience cares about and which examples to use. Now a salesperson can ask Hops for a customer email in the team chat and get one in the company's voice right away, written straight into the shared doc. The head of marketing spends her time on strategy instead of line edits. #5545. Breach Secure Now Launches MCP Connector, Putting Security Program Data to Work in ChatGPT, Claude and Microsoft Copilot

New connector helps MSPs prioritize client needs, create customized reports and demonstrate service value, while giving business leaders and employees greater visibility into security progress.

MORRISTOWN, N.J., Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Breach Secure Now (BSN), a provider of cybersecurity, AI awareness, productivity and compliance solutions delivered to small and midsize businesses (SMBs) through Managed Service Providers (MSPs), today announced the Breach Secure Now MCP, a new integration that brings BSN Portal Data directly into ChatGPT, Claude and Microsoft.

MSPs manage valuable security program data across their clients' portfolios, but finding the right information often means navigating multiple dashboards, pulling individual reports, and spending time organizing results. The Breach Secure Now MCP changes this process by allowing users to ask questions about their data in plain language, directly within familiar AI assistants.

The connector extends beyond MSP administrators, giving their clients business leaders and employees access to information appropriate to their BSN account permissions. MSPs can prioritize client needs and prepare for business reviews, leadership teams can evaluate security program performance, and employees can track their own security awareness progress.

Helping MSPs Turn Program Data into Action

For MSPs, the Breach Secure Now MCP provides a practical and highly impactful way to review security program data across their managed clients, identify accounts that need attention, prioritize outreach and prepare for Quarterly Business Reviews (QBRs).

Rather than reviewing individual client reports, MSPs can ask questions such as, "Which of my clients I call first, and why?"  The AI assistant can quickly retrieve and analyze available BSN Portal Data, helping partners identify priorities and turn information that previously required extensive manual reporting into useful summaries in minutes. MSPs can also generate customized client reports that bring together relevant security program information metrics, helping them demonstrate going value and have more productive client conversations.

"MSPs have a tremendous amount of valuable information available through the security programs they manage, but turning that information into meaningful client conversations takes time," said Art Gross, CEO of Breach Secure Now. "With the Breach Secure Now MCP, we're continuing our commitment to first-to-market innovation by making it easier for partners to understand where their clients need attention, show the progress they're making, and have more productive conversations about security. Just as importantly, we're giving business leaders and employees a way to better understand their own results."

Greater Visibility for Business Leaders and Employees

The benefits extend beyond MSP administrators to the organizations and employees they support.

Business leaders can use their AI assistants to review their organization's training participation, Employee Secure Score and aggregate phishing results. They can summarize program performance for leadership, identify areas that need attention, and determine where additional follow-up may be needed.

Employees can use their AI assistants to check their Employee Secure Score, review completed training and access their personal phishing history. They can also see how their score has changed over the past six weeks, giving them a clearer picture of their security awareness progress and where they may need to focus their attention.

Chris Gross, Sr AI Product Director, adds, "For years, partners have asked us for more flexibility in how they access and present their security program data," said Chris Gross, Senior Director of AI Product at Breach Secure Now. "With the Breach Secure Now MCP, they're no longer limited to predefined reports. They can ask their own questions, create tailored summaries, and use their AI assistants to build reports around what matters most to their clients. This opens up a whole new way for MSPs to put their data to work."

Secure, Role-Based Access to BSN Portal Data

The Breach Secure Now MCP uses Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard that enables AI assistants to connect securely with applications and data sources.

Users sign in with their existing BSN credentials, and access is limited to the information permitted by their BSN account role. MSP administrators can view data for their managed clients, client management can access organizational information, and employees can view their personal results.

The connector is read-only and does not change records within the BSN Portal.

"We're meeting our partners where they already work. BSN's MCP server brings portal data into everyday AI tools, so partners, company managers, and individual users can get the answers relevant to their role just by asking," said AL Lowenstein, CTO of Breach Secure Now.

Available Now, with Additional Capabilities Planned

The Breach Secure Now MCP is available now to BSN users with the appropriate account permissions and supports ChatGPT, Claude and Microsoft Copilot.

Development is already underway to expand the BSN Portal Data and reporting capabilities available through the connector, with additional enhancements planned for future releases.

The same connection will also support the upcoming BSN Skills Libraryâ¢, planned for Q1 2027. Building on BSN's commitment to employee education, the Skills Library will provide guided AI workflows built on proven frameworks, helping employees develop practical skills and apply AI across a wide range of business functions.

#5544. Anthropic targets an IPO valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, less than expected

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Investors were expecting roughly $1.5 trillion a week ago, but several large backers pressed for a lower number after AI stocks sold off

Anthropic launched the roadshow for its initial public offering on Tuesday, setting an expected price range of $70 to $78 a share for 825 million shares of Class A common stock.

Anthropic is selling 801,351,354 of those shares, and certain existing stockholders are selling the other 23,648,646. Anthropic will receive no proceeds from the stockholders' sales. The company also expects to give underwriters a 30-day option to buy up to 123,750,000 additional shares.

At the top of the range, Anthropic could carry a fully diluted valuation as high as $1.405 trillion, and the offering could raise as much as $64.35 billion before costs, according to CNBC. Anthropic is targeting a valuation near $1.33 trillion, and an offering priced at the midpoint would bring in upwards of $61 billion, according to The Wall Street Journal. CNN puts the midpoint valuation at about $1.1 trillion once options and unvested stock are counted.

Anthropic has applied to list its Class A stock on the Nasdaq $NDAQ Global Select Market under the symbol "ANT." A registration statement has been filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and must become effective before any stock can be sold. Copies of the preliminary prospectus are available from Goldman Sachs $GS and Morgan Stanley $MS. Trading could begin as soon as next week, according to CNN.

Anthropic has agreed to sell $26 billion of Class N common stock in a private placement to Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom $AVGO, Google $GOOGL, Micron $MU, Microsoft $MSFT, Nvidia $NVDA and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company at the IPO price, according to CNBC. Those shares will be unregistered and exempt from underwriter lock-up agreements.

In an amended filing, the company said sales through the first three quarters, ending Sept. 30, came to $33.24 billion, a jump of about 1,200% from a year earlier. It posted a net loss of $104 billion over that span, mostly from fair-value adjustments on its derivative liabilities and its convertible notes. Run-rate revenue stood at roughly $81 billion as of late October, an increase of $10 billion over the month before.

The valuation target is well below earlier expectations. Investors were expecting roughly $1.5 trillion a week ago, but several large backers pressed for a lower number after AI stocks sold off sharply last Thursday, according to The Wall Street Journal. A figure near $2 trillion was under discussion several months back.

#5542. Commvault unveils Recovery Studio, AgentRecover update and joint work with three partners

Data protection provider Commvault Systems Inc. today used its SHIFT 2026 customer event to unveil Recovery Studio, a new service that will automate the rebuilding of entire business applications after an outage or cyberattack.

Four other announcements cover recovery for artificial intelligence agents and joint work with Databricks Inc., Nvidia Corp. and Zscaler Inc.

AgentRecover, the company’s tool for reversing damage done by AI agents, is being extended to agents built on Microsoft Corp.’s Foundry and on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore from Amazon Web Services Inc. Databricks and Nvidia technology will draw on governed enterprise data from Commvault’s Data Activate service. The Zscaler agreement is a strategic partnership centered on AI security.

Recovery Studio goes after the manual work of restoring a business one piece at a time. Data alone does not get an application running again. Without the identities, configurations and infrastructure it depends on, an application can stay offline long after its files are back.

A large enterprise may have hundreds of applications and thousands of identities to bring up in sequence. Getting back to even a minimal level of operation takes 28 days on average under conventional approaches, according to Commvault research from last year.

In place of that manual work, the service uses automated runbooks that rebuild and validate each component in order. Commvault said the runbooks also restore identity systems and cloud configurations, firewall rules included. Threat scans can run inside a runbook on supported resources, and the results feed into the call on whether a service is ready to go back into production. Operational, disaster and cyber recovery all run from the same platform.

Pranay Ahlawat, Commvault’s chief technology and AI officer, called the launch “the DevOps moment for recovery.” He said one orchestrated flow can take over from the spreadsheets and war rooms that recovery teams lean on today.

The AgentRecover update moves the company’s agent protection onto the platforms where businesses build production agents. In September Commvault added protection for agent configurations that tools such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code store on employee laptops.

Phil Goodwin, research vice president at International Data Corp., said conventional recovery assumes a discrete set of data at one point in time. Agents break that assumption, because the agent, its data and the resources around it all have to come back “at machine speed,” he said.

On Bedrock AgentCore and Foundry, the software discovers each agent and maps the data, applications and infrastructure it interacts with. If an agent goes rogue, its activity log shows which systems it may have touched across platforms.

Restores target the agent and whatever it changed. Customers can also run AgentRecover with Commvault’s identity recovery and change auditing tools to trace the identities an agent acted through.

The Databricks and Nvidia announcements both build on Data Activate, which turns backup copies protected by Commvault into datasets for analytics and AI. Much of the data companies hold is unstructured and scattered across systems. In research from BARC published by DataHub in June, 70% of data and AI leaders said less than half of their unstructured data could be found and used for AI.

Commvault Data Activate for Databricks shares data under Commvault management into Databricks through OpenSharing. The data arrives as governed tables in Unity Catalog with its ownership, access permissions and lineage intact.

Updates keep flowing as source content changes or is deleted, and customers do not have to rebuild a connection to every original source. Alan Atkinson, chief business development officer at Commvault, said the aim is “turning protected data into an active business asset.”

Nvidia’s part, delivered as a reference design for software-as-a-service and software deployments, centers on retrieval. Nvidia NIM microservices and Nemotron Retriever, together with the Nvidia cuVS library used with Apache Solr, extract and organize Commvault-protected content so applications and agents can pull from it more easily. Data Activate keeps that content current as source files change, retention periods expire or permissions are revoked.

On the security side, Commvault and Zscaler listed AI discovery, runtime governance and agent detection and recovery as early areas of collaboration, and the companies did not announce a joint product or availability date. Zscaler’s Security for AI line polices how employees and agents use AI tools. Dhawal Sharma, Zscaler’s executive vice president of AI security and strategic initiatives, said organizations need to be “prepared to recover quickly if something goes wrong.”

Recovery Studio, AgentRecover’s Amazon Bedrock AgentCore support and the Databricks integration are all due to enter early access in December, the last of them in select Microsoft Azure regions. Foundry support comes sooner, with early access targeted for this month.

The Nvidia reference design is set to reach general availability in 2027 after an early release in December. Recovery Studio will be priced on the amount of data configured for orchestrated recovery, and Commvault plans general availability in the coming months.

A virtual edition of SHIFT follows on Nov. 18.

#5541. Moonshot AI rented restricted Nvidia AI chips inside China, documents show

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Filings valued the 32 Super Micro servers at 432 million yuan ($64.8 million); Moonshot disputed the documents' accuracy

Moonshot AI agreed in August to lease 32 Super Micro Computer servers fitted with Nvidia $NVDA's B300 chips, and filings locate the machines in China, according to Bloomberg. The documents were filed with Beijing regulators.

U.S. rules bar the chips from being shipped to China unless Washington has expressly approved the sale, and Bloomberg said it could not establish whether such approval existed. The filings assigned the servers a combined worth of 432 million yuan ($64.8 million). Moonshot challenged the reliability of the records.

"We neither participated in nor authorized the related financing or guarantee arrangements, and had no knowledge of them," a Moonshot spokesperson said in an emailed statement, according to Bloomberg. The spokesperson said Moonshot has no business relationship with Lingmeixin (Beijing) Technology Co., the server owner.

Bloomberg reviewed two financing contracts signed Aug. 4 by Lingmeixin and Beijing Zhongguancun Bank, the financier. Lingmeixin pledged the servers and 345.6 million yuan in earnings from a service contract with Beijing Dark Side of the Moon Technology Co., Moonshot's main entity, as collateral for a 200 million yuan ($30 million) loan, according to Bloomberg.

A Lingmeixin statement attached to the contracts said the hardware was designated for the Moonshot service contract. It said Moonshot "only has right to use the compute service, with no ownership of the equipment," according to Bloomberg. The contracts list the servers as stored in Qingyang, in western China.

The bank submitted the documents to a database run by the credit agency of the People's Bank of China on Aug. 6, according to Bloomberg. After Bloomberg sent requests for comment on Nov. 3, the database documents carried no mention of Moonshot. Lingmeixin and the bank did not respond to requests for comment.

An Nvidia spokesperson said the companies behind the purchase "are not Nvidia customers," according to Bloomberg. A Super Micro spokesperson said the company "does not conduct business with these entities," according to Bloomberg.

A White House official asserted, once Moonshot's Kimi K3 model came out, that the startup had obtained use of controlled Nvidia hardware, according to Bloomberg. The White House said in July that Moonshot had accessed Nvidia's Blackwell chips by way of a site in Thailand, according to CNBC.

Moonshot has also discussed renting capacity from neoclouds hosting Nvidia chips in Europe, according to CNBC, which cited four unnamed people familiar with the matter. Moonshot did not respond to CNBC's request for comment.

Chinese filings have exposed similar purchases before. Semi-Tech Leasing Group Co., a Chinese financing company controlled by local government entities, financed purchases of servers carrying restricted Nvidia chips. One contract covered 32 Asustek Computer servers with B300 chips, and most of the servers were listed as deployed in a China Mobile data center in Ningxia. Semi-Tech Leasing replaced its filings with redacted copies by the end of June, removing server model designations, supplier names and installation locations.
