#5539. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

#5538. Tessera Unveils Integrated LADAR- Based Perimeter Security Solution Combining AI Platform with Thermal Imaging and Intelligent Classification

Integrated solution pairs DFSL's laser-based LADAR sensors with Zorronet's LYBA AI command-and-control platform to detect, visually verify and classify events at short range, without RF radar emissions

NETANYA, Israel, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Tessera Defense and Homeland Security Inc. (NYSE American: HLSQ) ("Tessera" or the "Company") today announced the commercial launch of its integrated perimeter security solution that combines LADAR (laser detection and ranging) sensors from DFSL with Zorronet's command-and-control platform, powered by its LYBA AI core. DFSL and Zorronet are independent subsidiaries of Tessera.

The modular solution integrates precision LADAR-based optical detection with commercially available day/night and thermal PTZ cameras, supported by AI analytics. It is designed for detection ranges of approximately 30, 60 and 100 meters, targeting sites that need accurate short-range detection and classification, particularly where RF-based radar is restricted, unsuitable or undesirable.

Conventional perimeter systems detect movement and raise an alert, leaving operators to interpret each event. Tessera's solution is designed to take the next steps automatically.

When a DFSL LADAR sensor detects an object, it passes the object's location to LYBA, which can automatically point a compatible PTZ camera at the target. LYBA then applies computer vision and AI analytics to verify, classify and analyze the event, giving operators context rather than a bare motion alert.

Depending on the AI models selected and the imagery available, the system can be configured to:

The goal is to turn raw detection data into actionable operational intelligence that supports faster, better-informed security decisions.

Rather than a fixed set of detection rules, LYBA offers a library of existing AI models and operational scenarios, built to grow as customer requirements evolve. Organizations can select relevant scenarios, integrate compatible third-party and open-source models, and develop or fine-tune models for specialized applications.

For example, a customer can configure the system not only to detect a person entering a restricted area, but also to determine whether that person is accompanied by an animal, is carrying a potentially suspicious object, or is exhibiting a predefined behavior of interest. New or adapted models are validated through a controlled integration process before they are deployed.

The solution supports secure on-premises and isolated (air-gapped) deployments, so approved AI capabilities can run without continuous internet connectivity. Software and model updates are delivered through controlled maintenance procedures, allowing the system to evolve without replacing the underlying sensing and imaging hardware. This approach is intended to meet the cybersecurity and operational requirements of sensitive facilities while providing long-term technological flexibility.

Short-Range Detection Without RF Radar Emissions

Unlike radar, which transmits radio-frequency energy, DFSL's LADAR uses laser-based optical sensing to detect and locate objects, so the detection process itself requires no RF radar transmissions. This can be an important advantage at facilities where radar emissions are restricted, where RF-sensitive equipment is present, or where operators want to minimize additional RF transmissions. Associated communications equipment can be configured with wired connectivity to meet applicable site restrictions.

The solution is built around a camera-agnostic architecture that supports compatible, commercially available motorized PTZ cameras, including day/night and thermal models, rather than requiring proprietary imaging hardware from a single manufacturer.

DFSL's LADAR provides precise location and detection data, the camera provides visual observation and tracking, and LYBA fuses both into a single operational picture. Configurations can be tailored to coverage requirements, environmental conditions and applications, and new analytics and AI capabilities can be added over time without redesigning the detection infrastructure.

Part of Tessera's Integrated Security Strategy

"The challenge in modern security is no longer simply detecting movement. It is understanding what is happening, how significant it is, and how to respond," said Michael Oster, Chief Executive Officer of Tessera. "By combining DFSL's precision LADAR with Zorronet's AI capabilities, we are bringing complementary technologies together into a new generation of intelligent security solutions. What sets this approach apart is its flexibility: customers can select scenarios, add models and adapt the system as their requirements evolve, including in isolated and highly sensitive environments. This is Tessera's strategy in practice: turning advanced technologies into practical, scalable solutions for real-world security challenges."

About Tessera Defense and Homeland Security Inc. (Formerly BiomX Inc.)

The Tessera platform integrates cameras, sensors, detection technologies, AI and other security infrastructure to identify threats, understand events and coordinate response in real time. Tessera provides the technology, hardware and implementation expertise needed to tailor security solutions to the specific requirements of each site, helping customers deploy and optimize integrated security systems across critical infrastructure, energy, digital infrastructure and homeland security applications. #5537. Trump says he believes Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had no idea his affair was a spy

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The president said the FBI is looking into the matter while Nvidia's board investigates a foreign intelligence effort aimed at its CEO

President Donald Trump said Monday that Nvidia $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang told him he did not know the woman he had an extramarital affair with was an alleged spy for China. Trump said he believes Huang.

Trump told reporters at the White House that he called Huang earlier in the day “to see if he’s feeling all right.” Trump said he asked Huang whether he had any idea the woman was a spy. “He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’” Trump said, according to The Wall Street Journal. “I really believe him.”

Trump said he learned of the allegations "not too long ago." He called Huang an "honorable man" and added that the FBI is reviewing the issue.

“We’ll look into it,” Trump said, according to NBC News. “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

The Justice Department is conducting a criminal probe of Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based firm suspected of illegally funneling Nvidia AI chips to China, according to NBC News. NBC News also reported that the Justice Department’s National Security Division is heading the inquiry, working alongside the FBI and the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security. It is also scrutinizing individuals connected with Megaspeed, including the question of whether Beijing enlisted one of them as an operative.

That person is Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive who, according to NBC News, American intelligence officials now consider to be an operative working for China. She is not related to Jensen Huang. China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun called the allegation unsubstantiated.

Nvidia's board said Sunday it had begun an independent inquiry following reports that Huang had been singled out by a foreign intelligence operation. Huang said he had been "unfaithful to my wife," according to NBC News.

Trump said the intelligence had not come to his attention when Huang accompanied him on a trip to China last May, according to The Wall Street Journal. Pressed on whether he would broach the subject with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen later this month, Trump said, “I don’t think so.” He added, “I’m sure President Xi will ask me about it.”

Nvidia stock fell as much as 8% in early trading Monday after the board began its probe, which drew attention to the company's lack of a publicly named successor to Huang. Nvidia stock closed down 4.2% on Monday.

A Los Angeles law firm also brought a shareholder class action in San Jose, California, federal court, naming Nvidia and Huang as defendants, according to CNBC. The Rosen Law Firm suit contends that the defendants issued inaccurate or deceptive statements concerning the affair and the relationship between Nvidia and Megaspeed.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries pressed Monday for a thorough briefing on the controversy around Nvidia, according to NBC News.

#5536. Lumbra gets $25M in backing to help intelligence community deploy reliable AI agents

When it comes to matters of national security, it’s vitally important to ensure that the right intelligence gets to the right decision-makers, but doing this in today’s complex information technology environments is challenging, to say the least.

Enter the artificial intelligence startup Lumbra Inc., which has just raised $25 million in early-stage A funding to develop specialist autonomous agents tasked with sorting through the most sensitive data of all. Today’s Series A round was led by Point72 Ventures and Ansa Capital, with participation from seed round investor Costanoa.

Lumbra was founded last year by former Central Intelligence Agency officer Aaron Brown and ex-special forces infantry officer Michael Hiebert. Together, they’ve built a platform called LumbraOS, which is designed to orchestrate AI agents within high-consequence and ultra-secure computing environments, where risks of any kind simply cannot be tolerated.

Brown explained that LumbraOS was built from the ground up as a “model-neutral platform” that allows operators to mix and match various proprietary and open-weight AI models, assigning them different national security- and intelligence-related tasks. The platform is built on three key pillars: Nebula, StarChart and Astrolabe.

Nebula is the component tasked with managing agent orchestration, and works by tracing every “claim” generated by AI agents back to the primary source data behind that claim, so that domain experts can validate their outputs before decisions are made. StarChart is a dynamic knowledge graph that links disparate insights across multiple datasets through embedded sensitivity tags. Meanwhile, Astrolabe enforces governance policies and continuously evaluates each agent after benchmarking their performance prior to deployment to monitor for any alarming behavior.

Traditional AI systems developers struggle for years to ensure they meet the most rigorous federal security standards, but Brown and Hiebert say they developed LumbraOS specifically for classified computing environments. Just two months after launching their platform, they quietly landed a multimillion-dollar contract with an unnamed U.S. intelligence agency, with their AI agents operating on a top-secret defense network within just six months.

Impressed with the startup’s technology, the Pentagon followed up by naming Lumbra as one of two companies that underpins its Agent Network project, and one of seven “pace-setting projects” within its broader AI Acceleration strategy.

Following this traction, Lumbra’s co-founders believe there is potential for LumbraOS to expand beyond the intelligence community. They’re targeting enterprises in high-stakes industries such as healthcare, finance and law, where sensitive data leaks are deal breakers.

Brown said most organizations in these industries only use autonomous agents for singular tasks, if at all. That’s because they lack the tools to make those agents controllable, transparent and reliable enough at large scale. With its traceable audit logs and strict governance controls, Lumbra thinks it can help organizations to deploy agents safely across their networks to automate more complex workloads.

“The organizations that get agents right will spend less time telling them what to do and more time deciding what they may touch and what their work must prove,” Brown said. “Thousands of agents working a question together can find an insight while there’s still time to act on it. Lumbra exists to give decision-makers an advantage at the moment of decision.”

To target the enterprise, Lumbra plans to use the funds from today’s round to expand its engineering and product development teams and accelerate its go-to-market operations.

Ansa Capital Managing Partner Marco DeMeireles said the problem of trust and verifiability is the biggest barrier to adoption for AI agents in high-stakes environments. “Lumbra has demonstrated its ability to bring these capabilities into production across some of the most demanding environments within the U.S. government,” he said. “We believe these same capabilities will become foundational to how the world’s most critical enterprises deploy AI.”

#5534. T. Rowe Price warned Treasury yields won't peak until a recession hits

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Arif Husain, the firm's head of global fixed income, said the Fed could raise rates until something breaks

T. Rowe Price $TROW said Treasury yields won't peak until the U.S. economy enters a recession, according to Bloomberg.

"Yields won't truly peak until there is a recession," said Arif Husain, who leads global fixed income at the firm, in a report, according to Bloomberg. "There is a chance that the Fed could hike until something breaks — essentially an overtightening policy mistake."

Husain regards inflation as the bigger near-term worry, ahead of the country's fiscal problems. He said the Federal Reserve may need to lift borrowing costs higher than markets currently anticipate.

He also flagged the possibility of a bear flattening in the U.S. yield curve, in which short-dated debt sells off harder than long-dated debt. He added that it would hardly shock him if the curve inverted "in the relatively near future."

Husain pointed to another potential trigger for yields topping out: developed-market governments taking tangible action to get their finances in order. "With yields on French government bonds climbing rapidly in October — to the point that some French corporate bonds yielded less than the sovereign — I'm watching to see if any other countries are learning the lesson," he wrote, according to Bloomberg.

Husain said the Treasury gains in October came as traders closed out bearish bets, not because investors were rushing back to havens. He said he would need to see "a lot more evidence — outside of a seasonally illiquid period" to believe the safe-haven explanation, according to Bloomberg.

The benchmark 10-year yield reached a peak of 5.36% this year, driven by inflation worries stoked by the Iran war. It then slid to roughly 4.86% after a selloff in technology shares drew investors back to sovereign debt. Husain initially floated a 6% 10-year yield less than two years ago, at a point when the market was tilting toward Fed rate cuts.

Yields had been hitting 24-year highs of 5.365% on the 10-year and 5.733% on the 30-year before pulling back after well-received government bond auctions. Money markets were pricing in three rate increases over the following 12 months.

Consumer prices then rose 3.7% over the 12 months ending in September, above the 3.6% economists had forecast. The 10-year yield rose to 5.304% that day.

#5533. F-Secure identifies 26 ways AI can harm consumers, and where to stop them

New AI Harms Taxonomy traces how harm moves through AI systems,from misleading chatbot answers to compromised autonomous agents, and identifies where defenses can intervene

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AI now shapes how we search, communicate, decide and run our digital lives. But when it goes wrong, how does it actually hurt people? F-Secure's new AI Harms Taxonomy maps 26 distinct harms to consumers, tracing the path each one takes to reach a person. The result is a clear view of where protections can step in, and who is in the best position to help.

Developed by Dr. Megan Squire, Principal Threat Intelligence Researcher at F-Secure, the taxonomy tackles a blind spot in how AI risk is discussed. Most frameworks list what could potentially go wrong, but stop short of connecting those harms to the systems and companies that could prevent them. F-Secure's research goes further by mapping every layer between an AI-enabled threat and its impact on a consumer, then pinpointing where defenses need to go.

"As AI systems become more capable, the consequences of their mistakes can extend well beyond a bad answer," said Dr. Squire. "The people building them have a responsibility to understand how they can fail and who gets hurt when they do, and to put safeguards in place before that harm happens."

The taxonomy reflects how the risks themselves are changing. It used to be a criminal going after a person directly, but now AI sits in the middle, which adds new players and new ways for things to go wrong. An assistant acting on someone's behalf can be manipulated into doing damage, and a chatbot can mislead with complete confidence. Underneath, the trouble often starts in how an AI handles instructions and memory, or in the other services it's connected to.

The research currently maps 26 harms across five relationship types and 19 intermediary layers, with 24 defenses designed to address risks at different points. Examples range from AI-generated voice and video impersonation to agents making harmful financial decisions, exposing personal information or acting on outdated context. It also examines attacks in which malicious instructions are hidden in content an AI system processes, potentially influencing what an agent does or what a chatbot tells a user.

One of the framework's central findings is that responsibility for preventing AI harm is spread across several parties. Some risks can be handled by security software on a person's own device. Others have to be dealt with further upstream, by the companies that build AI products and the systems behind them, including how an AI remembers things and which other services it connects to. Sorting out which is which makes it clear where a defense belongs and who has to build it. It also undercuts the idea that people can stay safe on their own just by spotting suspicious content or double-checking what an AI tells them.

This question of who's responsible gets more urgent as AI moves from producing information to acting on it. A chatbot that gets an answer wrong can mislead someone, but at least that person is part of the exchange. An agent with access to a person's accounts and the services linked to them can cause real consequences without that kind of back-and-forth. Protections need to be built around what these systems actually do, which starts with understanding how the two differ.

This research is part of a wider effort at F-Secure to build trust into the AI era. F-Secure Trust, announced alongside a strategic alliance with Quantum AI Lab QuTwo, is the company's work on protecting people in a world where AI agents increasingly act for them. TrustGuard is designed to help protect people during AI interactions, while TrustPath aims to secure their digital journeys from discovery to delivery. The AI Harms Taxonomy gives that work a research foundation by spelling out the risks the protections need to address, and it makes clear that meaningful safeguards also depend on the companies building and running AI systems.

Today's digital threats go far beyond just scams. F-Secure's Illuminate Research team studies people and technology as they actually interact, exploring the messy realities of trust, deception, and online resilience in the AI era. The AI Harms Taxonomy is available on the Illuminate Research Hub.

F-Secure is a human-first, AI-powered consumer cyber security experience company with 38 years of expertise in tackling digital threats. We help digital service providers turn trust into a high-value growth engine â protecting their customers while enabling them to live their best digital lives in a world of relentless, AI-driven scams. With billions of digital interactions secured each year, tens of millions of consumers protected globally, and over $10bn in partner value created, we deliver proven impact at scale.

The latest letters renew congressional pressure following months of investigations and previous requests for information. November 30 marks the initial document production deadline, while January 4, 2027, is the final deadline for voluntary compliance. Blumenthal, in his investigation, warned that the Senate could pursue alternative measures if the companies fail to cooperate.

🇺🇸 BREAKING: U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal sends letter to Tether, Binance, and two Trump-linked crypto firms demanding records in the ongoing Senate investigations before January 4, 2027.The incoming chair of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations is examining… pic.twitter.com/MwFVngVngm

For now, the letters do not announce subpoenas or formal enforcement actions. Instead, they establish a final window for the companies to provide records before the subcommittee considers further steps.

Blumenthal currently serves as the ranking member of the investigative panel. He is expected to become its chair when Democrats assume control of the Senate subcommittee. This transition could strengthen his ability to pursue compulsory document requests.

The Binance inquiry has already faced several rounds of correspondence. Blumenthal first requested information about the exchange’s compliance practices and potential Iran-linked transactions in February 2026.

He renewed those demands in April, questioning whether Binance had provided misleading information about its handling of suspicious transactions. The exchange has disputed allegations surrounding its compliance practices.

The Tether investigation gained momentum following a September 28 report from Democratic investigators on the Senate subcommittee. The report examined 846 cryptocurrency wallets sanctioned or targeted for seizure because of their alleged connections to Iran and regional proxy groups.

Investigators found that 84% of those wallets had transacted exclusively or almost exclusively in USDT. They described Tether’s stablecoin as a significant financial channel within Iran’s shadow banking network.

Tether has pushed back against the findings, arguing that its compliance teams proactively freeze suspicious wallets. CEO Paolo Ardoino also claimed the company froze Iran-linked addresses an average of four weeks before official sanctions designations.

Meanwhile, the Trump investigation focuses on his two crypto ventures, World Liberty Financial and Fight Fight Fight LLC. Blumenthal originally opened the inquiry in May 2025 following concerns about potential conflicts of interest involving Trump.

Investigators are examining foreign investments, financial relationships with overseas entities, and potential violations of government ethics requirements. Fight Fight Fight LLC operates the Official Trump memecoin, while World Liberty Financial is associated with the Trump family’s crypto business.

The senator also hosted a public forum in July 2026 examining the Trump family’s crypto companies. That proceeding included testimony from TRUMP investors who reported losing thousands of dollars.

The latest requests connect two major political and financial investigations. One examines potential sanctions-related crypto activity, while the other focuses on foreign money and presidential business interests.

The January deadline could become a significant test of congressional oversight. Blumenthal will soon lead the investigative panel as it pursues records from companies connected to some of the biggest names in crypto.

#5531. October CPI rose 0.4%, but a funding lapse last year leaves most annual rates unpublished

Free daily briefing on global business news.

BLS published 12-month changes for a few items, including gasoline up 37.4%, after missing October 2025 survey data

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Tuesday that the consumer price index for all urban consumers rose 0.4% in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, after a 0.6% increase in September. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3%, matching its gains in September and August.

Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had forecast a 0.3% overall increase and a 0.2% core gain, according to CNBC.

The bureau collected no survey data for October 2025 because of a lapse in appropriations, so it could not publish October 2025 indexes for most CPI series. The agency is therefore unable to publish 12-month changes for October 2026 for indexes that lack that data.

A few annual changes were published. Gasoline rose 37.4% over 12 months, used cars and trucks fell 3.3%, and new vehicles rose 0.7%. Prices for all items rose an estimated 4% over 12 months and core prices rose 2.8%, according to calculations by The New York Times.

The shelter index rose 0.3% in October and accounted for over 30% of the monthly increase in all items. The food index rose 0.5%. The energy index rose 0.7% after a 5.2% jump in September.

Gasoline rose 1.0% on a seasonally adjusted basis, though prices fell 0.7% before seasonal adjustment. The electricity index rose 0.9%, while the natural gas index fell 0.8%.

Used cars and trucks fell 1.2% in October after a 0.7% gain in September. The communication index fell 0.1%. Recreation rose 0.8%, motor vehicle insurance rose 0.7% and medical care rose 0.3%.

The two-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.69%, a gain of more than a tenth of a percentage point.

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said in remarks on Tuesday that a half-point rate increase in December could be warranted if core inflation came in at 0.3% or higher, according to The New York Times. The Fed meets Dec. 8-9.

The bureau will publish the November CPI report on Dec. 10 at 8:30 a.m. ET.

#5529. PuppyGraph raises $10M to let AI agents query enterprise data as a graph

Graph query engine startup PuppyGraph said today it has raised $10 million in new funding to build out its enterprise go-to-market operation.

The round follows the general release of version 1.0 of its software. PuppyGraph provides a query engine that lets companies treat data already sitting in their warehouses and lakehouses as a single graph, without first moving it into a separate graph database. The company says artificial intelligence agents running on it can work across 3,000 enterprise tables and get graph query results back in under a second.

Agent projects tend to hit trouble once they leave the pilot stage, according to PuppyGraph. The company’s own example asks which critical systems an attacker could reach from a compromised account, a question that means tracing how identities and permissions connect across thousands of tables in several systems.

A proof of concept might cover 30 to 50. Teams that scale past that find schema descriptions alone eating into an agent’s context window, and PuppyGraph said queries running several relationships deep can stall until they time out.

Data teams setting up PuppyGraph 1.0 start from a schema that an AI-assisted tool drafts out of their existing tables. Once they have approved it, users can put questions to the graph in plain English.

PuppyGraph has its own agent for that, and the Model Context Protocol lets companies bring in the AI tools they already use. Agents are kept from guessing how the data fits together. Any agent that references a relationship nobody set up gets its query bounced, and the error that comes back is written for the agent to act on.

When PuppyGraph connects to Snowflake Inc. or Databricks Inc. it can obtain short-lived credentials tied to the user’s identity, so nobody has to hand over long-lived keys. Row-level permissions configured on the data still apply, and the company says it checks them at each hop of a traversal.

“The insights of enterprise data will soon be generated by agents,” said Weimo Liu (pictured), co-founder and chief executive of PuppyGraph. “Users will expect to ask questions that cross departments and systems, beyond the workflows someone built into a dashboard.”

PuppyGraph’s customer list includes Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Palo Alto Networks Inc., and the announcement also named Coinbase Global Inc., Datadog Inc. and Trend Micro Inc. as customers. Xinyu Liu, a staff software engineer at Coinbase, said that because the exchange connects straight to tables it already keeps in Snowflake and Databricks, “standing up a new graph is a schema definition, not a data migration.” Weimo Liu worked as a software engineer at Google LLC before co-founding the Santa Clara-based company.

PuppyGraph’s annual recurring revenue grew sevenfold over the past year, by the startup’s count. No dollar figure was disclosed.

Particle Future and defy.vc led the Series A round. It is the second time defy.vc has led a round for PuppyGraph, after a $5 million seed round in November 2024. PuppyGraph will also put some of the new money into engineering.

Amy Yin, a partner at defy.vc, said writing a query is now a job a user can hand to Anthropic PBC’s Claude. Executing it across billions of relationships still “takes serious engineering,” in her view.

Developers can download a free version of PuppyGraph with a single Docker command and no sign-up form, and the company says it takes about 10 minutes to go from deployment to a first query. Investors have now put $15 million into the startup.

#5528. AI's gains concentrate at a few firms: 10 findings on pay, hiring and productivity

Free daily briefing on global business news.

PwC's 2026 AI jobs barometer shows productivity, hiring and pay gains pooling at a few firms and workers. Here are 10 findings.

The argument over AI and work used to turn on whether the technology would ever reach ordinary jobs. That argument is settled. Employers and workers already use AI every day, in offices, call centers and finance departments. Engineers are no longer the only workers who feel the technology, since nearly 40% of jobs around the world are open to change from AI, according to the IMF. When that much work is open to a new technology, asking whether it will change jobs no longer tells anyone much. The questions worth asking are who collects its gains and who is left out.

Using AI at work has become common, but its payoff for employment is harder to find. About 43% of U.S. workers regularly use AI on the job, according to Indeed Hiring Lab. The spread of AI-related skills has done nothing so far to lift employment, according to the IMF. Wide use of a tool and broad benefit from it are not the same thing. That leaves open where AI's gains are going, and the more revealing story is which companies and which workers are capturing them.

PwC's 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer set out to measure how AI was reshaping jobs, skills, pay and company productivity. PwC looked at a small group of superstar companies, the pay premium for AI skills and junior jobs that now ask for senior abilities. Jobs, skills, pay and output are the four things workers and employers feel most directly, so they are the right places to look for where AI's gains are going. Some of those gains reach across sectors, while others collect at a handful of companies or among a narrow group of workers. A gap between leaders and laggards shows who is ahead, but it does not explain why. "Careful interpretation of this chart is necessary – this is not to say AI is causing these impacts," PwC said in a note on one of its charts. That caution applies to every gap that follows. Set beside independent data, each finding shows how far a given gain reaches.

The companies most exposed to AI are opening a wide productivity lead over the rest, and that lead is getting bigger fast. Since 2022, their advantage has tripled, and their productivity now grows 40% faster than that of the companies least exposed to AI, according to PwC. Those firms are not simply ahead of their peers. They are moving further away from them each year. For a company, heavy exposure to AI has gone together with pulling ahead.

Across whole industries, the gains look far calmer. The Federal Reserve Board reports that industries more exposed to AI do have higher productivity growth, but their trends have stayed steady over time instead of widening. Information, finance, and professional and business services rank among the industries most exposed to AI. AI tools are built for this desk-based work, so any broad gain from AI should show up there first. The two findings fit together. A sharply widening lead for some companies, alongside a steady trend for their industries, suggests the gains are concentrated in particular firms within those sectors rather than spread across them.

Economists studying the national data see the same split between company results and wider growth. Paul E. Soto, Mason Thieu and Jeffrey S. Allen, economists at the Federal Reserve Board, said the pattern is "suggestive of micro-level productivity gains not adding up in aggregate." Strong results at the leading companies are not yet visible as a broad rise in output. The productivity gap is best read as a measure of how far some companies have pulled ahead, not of how much AI has raised productivity across the economy.

If the gains sit with particular companies, the next question is whether every exposed firm shares in them or mainly those at the top of the group.

Companies that are heavily exposed to AI do not all benefit equally. Within that group, a handful of firms have pulled far ahead of everyone else. The top fifth of the most AI-exposed firms average 163% productivity growth, far above the rest of their own group, according to PwC. Many companies are exposed to AI, but the biggest productivity gains show up at the firms at the very top of that group. The 163% figure describes what a few leading companies achieved, not what exposed companies in general have managed.

Across the wider economy, firms that use AI more heavily see gains that are real but small. Economists Tina Highfill and Jon D. Samuels of the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, or BEA, estimate that each additional percentage point of workers who use AI frequently goes with only about 0.1% to 0.2% higher real output. Compared with that everyday range, the top firms' result is an extreme case, and other companies should not expect to match it. Even a more generous outside estimate stays in single digits. A study of European firms by Aldasoro and colleagues estimated a 4% rise in labor productivity, according to Aldasoro figures reported by BEA. That estimate falls far below the top tier's average. Managers planning their own AI spending should treat the 163% figure as an exceptional result that a few firms reached, not as a return they can count on.

The largest productivity gains so far appear at a small set of leading companies, and the next question is whether workers at AI-heavy employers share in them through hiring and pay.

Many people expect the companies that lean hardest on AI to cut jobs, but the most exposed firms are adding workers faster than anyone else. Those companies grew their staff by 52%, compared with 36% at less exposed firms, according to PwC. The employers with the most AI in their work are the ones hiring most quickly. They are also paying their people more, with pay rising 24% at the most exposed firms against 17% elsewhere. Staff at these companies are getting larger raises as well as more colleagues. At these employers, heavy exposure to AI has gone together with growth in both the size of the workforce and what it earns.

The upside is real, but it belongs to the workers at a particular set of employers. PwC takes a hopeful view of AI and jobs more generally. "Far from being a job killer, AI may actually be a job expander," PwC said. The word "may" marks that view as a possibility, not a finding about jobs across the economy. The faster hiring and bigger raises took place inside the exposed companies themselves. The figures show those firms growing faster than their peers, not the job market as a whole getting larger. For a worker, the lesson is that the stronger hiring and better pay are found at AI-heavy employers. That pattern gives one more sign that the rewards from AI are collecting at the companies where AI use is already concentrated.

Employers wanted AI specialists far more than they wanted workers in general in 2025. They posted 68.9% more openings for AI specialists that year, while they posted only 8.6% more openings across all jobs, according to PwC. That gap shows where companies are putting their money, which is into a narrow group of workers they consider worth competing for. Companies can post many openings for a skill without hiring many people for it, though. How many people end up holding these jobs is what matters to someone looking for work.

Data science, one of the occupations most closely tied to AI, is expected to keep growing, but it will supply a fairly small number of new positions. BLS projects about 82,500 more data scientist jobs in 2034 than in 2024. That is real growth for the field, yet it adds far fewer positions than the larger tech occupations will. Strong demand for a small pool of workers fits the larger pattern of AI's rewards collecting among a few. For most job seekers, the specialist boom is worth following, but it is not where their next job is likely to come from.

The largest projected gain in tech jobs goes to a mainstream role. BLS projects about 267,700 new software developer jobs over the same decade, the largest numerical gain among the occupations in its chart. The efficiency that companies want from AI is also expected to hold down routine work, with about 153,700 fewer customer service representative jobs projected. That decline reflects fewer future openings as companies use AI to handle the work more efficiently, not layoffs that have already happened.

The rush for AI specialists is the most visible part of a larger shift, and for most workers what matters is whether their own job is among those growing or those shrinking.

Employers outside engineering now ask for AI skills when they hire. "AI specialist hiring is rising in all sectors," PwC said. Marketing shows how far that demand has moved from software. Over 2025, employers went from mentioning AI in 8.4% of marketing job postings to 14.9%, according to Indeed Hiring Lab. For a worker in marketing or another business function, AI has become a subject employers raise in hiring, not a concern for the IT department alone.

Even in the field where employers mention AI most, they hire mainly for other work. In data and analytics, the leading field, employers mentioned AI in 45% of postings in December 2025, according to Indeed Hiring Lab. A high share in one field shows where employers want AI skills most. It does not mean the jobs in that field have become AI jobs.

In tech, employers mention AI in a large share of postings at a time when they advertise far fewer jobs. The number of tech openings employers post is 34% lower than before the pandemic, according to Indeed Hiring Lab. For someone looking for tech work, a high AI share describes what the remaining openings require, not a rise in hiring.

Across the whole U.S. job market, AI appears in only a small minority of job ads. Employers mentioned AI in 4.2% of all U.S. job postings in December 2025, the highest level on Indeed's AI tracker, according to Indeed Hiring Lab. The leading sectors show where employers are changing what they ask of new hires.

Most U.S. job ads still make no mention of AI.

Employers keep raising what they will pay for AI skills. PwC finds that employers advertise about 62% more pay on average for workers with AI skills, a bigger premium than a year earlier. A premium that grows from one year to the next shows that employers value these skills more now than they did before. For anyone deciding what to learn next, this rising pay is the clearest sign of where the money in AI sits today.

AI skills earn workers far more than the usual reward for learning something new. Employers in the U.K. and U.S. offer only about 3% more pay in job ads that ask for one new skill, according to the IMF. Workers who stack several new skills do better, and U.K. employers offer up to 15% more pay when they ask for four or more. Even that reward falls well short of what employers pay for AI skills. Employers appear to treat AI skill as a category of its own, apart from the general reward workers get for keeping up.

Few job ads ask for new skills of any kind. Employers in advanced economies ask for a new skill in only about 1 in 10 job ads, according to the IMF. Pay boosts tied to fresh skills therefore reach a limited part of the job market. A rising AI premium means workers who hold those skills are getting paid well. It does not show that AI is lifting pay for most people.

The premium may not last, either. The IMF warns that AI may automate many IT tasks. If that happens, employers' demand for tech skills need not turn into equal demand for the specialists who hold them.

The premium is a guide to where AI pays today, not a promise that the pay will last.

Employers are changing the skills they ask for much faster in some jobs than in others. In the jobs most exposed to AI, employers change their skill requirements 2.2 times as fast as in less exposed work, and that gap is 75% wider than it was a year earlier, according to PwC. For someone in one of those jobs, the knowledge that got them hired becomes outdated sooner, and they have less time to learn what replaces it. In a single year, exposed roles have moved further from other work in how quickly their skill demands shift. The pressure to keep learning is therefore uneven. Workers in the jobs most exposed to AI face most of it, while people in less exposed roles deal with a slower and more familiar rate of change.

The direction of that gap matters more than its size in any one year. A gap that widens from one year to the next points toward a job market that is splitting further apart, not one that is settling into a new balance. For workers in exposed roles, a single round of retraining is unlikely to be enough if employers there keep revising what they want. For workers elsewhere, the skills they hold today will stay useful for longer. Employers in exposed fields face a similar choice between training their staff more often and hiring new people whose skills are more current.

If the skills in exposed jobs keep changing this quickly, the next question is which abilities keep their value through all that change.

The common assumption about AI at work is that employers hand tasks to software and the job gets smaller. In the jobs most exposed to AI, the tasks employers are adding depend far more on human abilities than the tasks added in other work. Those new tasks rely on empathy, creativity and presence 2.5 times more than elsewhere, according to PwC. Workers in these roles are taking on more of the work that involves understanding other people, coming up with original ideas and being there in person. A job that is highly exposed to AI is therefore not simply a smaller job. These roles are gaining duties, and the duties they gain are ones that people perform better than software.

For someone in an exposed field, the finding shows where to put effort. Learning to use AI tools has value, but technical fluency alone does not match the kind of new work these jobs are adding. A worker who learns to read a client's needs, propose fresh approaches and handle difficult situations face to face is preparing for the tasks employers are actually assigning. Those abilities are also harder for software to take over than routine technical work.

Workers who build these abilities may find they hold a steadier place in fields that AI is reshaping quickly, because the work employers keep adding there is the work machines handle worst.

In the jobs most exposed to AI, employers now want junior hires who bring senior skills from their first day. PwC finds that junior roles in those jobs are seven times as likely to demand skills traditionally expected of senior staff, and that postings with these upgraded requirements have risen 35% since 2019. Employers have steadily made senior abilities a larger part of what they expect from a first hire. CNBC reports that junior staff under Orlando Bravo, founder of Thoma Bravo, now spend far less of their week on financial models and comparison work than they once did. "If you define the role of an associate as just doing a spreadsheet, you don't need that, but our associates are now calling on companies a lot more," Bravo said. In his account, junior staff at his firm gave up the most routine part of the job and kept a more demanding one.

A tougher job description shows what employers want from juniors, not that they want more of them. Employers raised those demands during a year of job cuts linked to AI, with over 50,000 U.S. layoffs in 2025 tied to the technology, according to CNBC. Bravo is hiring more people for the first time in his career, but he is describing his own firm rather than the wider market. He sees young workers taking on bigger work sooner. Given the layoffs, the same higher demands may also mean fewer junior jobs and a harder path into them.

Young workers who already have AI skills get paid for meeting those higher demands. Employers will pay young hires who bring AI skills as much as 25% more, according to Randstad figures reported by CNBC. That extra pay goes only to those who arrive with the skills. The British government treats the problem as one of job design. Liz Kendall, the U.K. technology secretary, says the government will train people and change how starting jobs are built. A government that plans to rework the first job confirms that the change reaches the starting role itself.

A first job now demands more than it used to, and who gets one depends more on the skills young workers bring on their first day.

The gaps between companies, skills and pay add up to a split that a worker can feel directly, in which jobs still offer a way up. That divide now runs between kinds of work, not only between firms. "Our analysis suggests opportunity is migrating from democratised roles toward professionalised and low AI exposure roles (with exceptions)," PwC said. The hedge in parentheses matters, because it marks the shift as a direction rather than a rule. Still, the track a worker lands on may depend more on the kind of job they hold than on the company that employs them.

U.S. government forecasters expect both tracks to take shape over the next decade. BLS projects that data scientist jobs will grow 34.6% from 2025 to 2035, a fast rise in exactly the kind of professionalized work that opportunity is moving toward. On the other side, it projects the loss of 752,100 office and administrative support jobs, the routine work that automation can take over. In these projections, fast growth comes in a specialized field and steep losses come in routine office work. That pattern points the same way as PwC's reading of where opportunity is heading.

The largest source of new U.S. jobs has little to do with AI. Private health care and social assistance will account for about 37.0% of projected new jobs, driven by an aging population and chronic illness, according to BLS. Exposure to AI matters for which track some jobs end up on, but a worker who weighs options by AI alone misses where much of the hiring will happen. Both tracks rest on forecasts, so the shrinking one is a projection to watch, not a settled outcome.

#5527. Solana Validator Admission Ticket: Who Fell Short After Alpenglow, and How Marinade Responded

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

StakeThat +MEV went into one of Solana's first Alpenglow epochs with about 137,000 SOL staked with it and 0.8169 SOL in its vote account. The new admission ticket required 0.8198 SOL. It was 0.003 SOL short.

That's the first post-activation picture of Solana's Validator Admission Ticket. Most stake made it through without trouble, but a small group of validators keeps dropping in and out, often by amounts smaller than a typical transaction fee. At least one large stake program changed its delegation code hours before activation so its stake wouldn't stay with those validators. Marinade's published validator snapshots for epochs 1063 to 1067 show who fell short and what happened next.

According to Solana's BLS Pubkey and VAT page, Alpenglow has been active on mainnet since epoch 1064, which began around 13:36 UTC on October 21. From then on, each validator's vote account pays a 0.8 SOL Validator Admission Ticket at the start of every epoch. The fee is burned, and it pays for the following epoch. The first charge, at the start of epoch 1064, covered epoch 1065.

The rules are strict. If the fee can't be paid, Solana's page says, "your validator does not vote or produce blocks in the next epoch." Validators without a registered BLS key, or outside the top 2,000 by stake, are also excluded. Delegators to an excluded validator earn no inflation rewards for that epoch. The page also stresses that the balance "has to stay funded, not be funded once."

The vote account also has to stay above its rent-exempt minimum. In Marinade's data, the full requirement works out to 0.8197612 SOL.

Marinade publishes the inputs to its stake auction every epoch in a public pipeline repository. The input data checks whether each validator's vote account holds enough to cover the next epoch's ticket. Each snapshot covers about 670 validators and roughly 438 million SOL of stake.

Before activation, in the epoch 1063 snapshot, 33 validators holding 7.63 million SOL, or 1.74% of stake, were below the ticket balance. Once Alpenglow went live, that number fell quickly: 15 validators with 1.55 million SOL (0.35%) in epoch 1064, then 19 with 1.15 million (0.26%) in epoch 1065, the first epoch the ticket actually paid for. By epoch 1066 it was 13 validators with 790,000 SOL (0.18%), and by epoch 1067 just 8 with 710,000 SOL (0.16%).

The epoch 1063 count matches a figure in Marinade's own code history. A commit on October 21 notes that its new gate "refuses the 33 validators with vat_eligible false" in the 1063 snapshot.

The biggest pre-activation gaps were fixed in time. An unnamed validator with 2.05 million SOL of stake, Temporal Emerald with 1.23 million and Bitget Wallet with 593,000 were all below the ticket balance in epoch 1063. All three had topped up by the next snapshot. Of the 33 flagged before activation, 25 had recovered by epoch 1064.

So the fee didn't remove a large share of stake. The balance check affected less than 2% of stake at its peak, and about 0.16% by epoch 1067.

The validators that did fall short show a pattern: many of them nearly had enough.

Because the ticket is charged every epoch, a validator that tops up just enough to pass once will fail again an epoch later unless it adds more. Between epochs 1064 and 1067, between 3 and 11 validators fell below the threshold each epoch, while a similar number recovered.

The shortfalls also cut across setups. Every validator flagged in epoch 1067 runs either Agave 4.3.x, the client release the migration required, or the latest Firedancer build. Software readiness wasn't the issue. Keeping the balance funded was.

Solana offers a fix: routing block revenue to the vote account through solana vote-update-commission-collector. That keeps the account funded automatically, though the change takes two epochs to apply.

The bigger story is how stake programs reacted. Marinade, one of Solana's largest delegation programs, changed its auction code in pull request #153, merged at about 06:47 UTC on October 21, roughly seven hours before Alpenglow activated.

The change adds a new disqualifying condition, vatIneligible. A validator whose vat_eligible flag is false "gets no SAM and no backstop stake," because "Agave then pays its stakers no inflation rewards for the epoch." A null value never disqualifies a validator. The check currently tests only the SIMD-0357 balance, not BLS key registration.

The first version applied the rule only in Alpenglow epochs. Marinade's developers then caught a timing problem. Agave starts charging the ticket at the 1063-to-1064 boundary, and "a stake move made in epoch E takes effect in E+1," so the original rule "left Marinade stake on refused validators for epochs 1064 and 1065." The merged version refuses ineligible validators in every epoch.

The snapshots confirm it worked. In the epoch 1064 snapshot, 192,762 SOL of Marinade stake sat on ineligible validators, nearly all of it on one unnamed validator. By epoch 1065, that had dropped to 2,407 SOL, and by epoch 1066 to 10 SOL. A later commit gives the rule its own label and call to action in Marinade's interface, so operators can see why they've been excluded.

Marinade, in short, turned a protocol fee into a delegation rule of its own. A validator that misses one ticket loses an epoch of rewards, and it also loses Marinade stake until its balance recovers.

Before activation, Solana Compass reported that a community tracker flagged 45% of stake as not ready two days ahead of epoch 1064, mostly validators on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1. The following day, that had dropped to 20.3%.

Marinade's snapshots show the software gap closing much as those warnings suggested it needed to. Stake on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1 fell from 6.56% in epoch 1063 to 0.08% by epoch 1067. Firedancer operators, who had to switch to Agave for the migration, dropped from 11.0% of stake to 5.9% in epoch 1064. They then came back strongly, reaching 17.2% by epoch 1067, well above their pre-migration share.

The large readiness gap was about software and keys, and it was mostly closed by the time it mattered. The fee gap was always small.

For most delegators, nothing changed: more than 99.8% of stake sits with validators that keep their tickets paid. For those delegated to the few that don't, the cost is clear: no inflation rewards for that epoch, and in Marinade's case, stake moved elsewhere.

The protocol sets one requirement: 0.8 SOL in the vote account every epoch. Stake programs are now adding their own rules on top, starting with Marinade's. Validators that keep running near the threshold will keep losing epochs of rewards, and possibly delegations, until they keep a buffer or automate funding.

#5526. Accent bias: AI models penalize certain speakers in interviews and tests, UW study finds

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 2:50 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 2:50 pm

Picture two job candidates giving the same answer to the same interview question, word for word. One has an American accent. The other has a Nigerian accent. Ask a leading AI model to score them, and the American will likely come out ahead.

That’s the gist of new research from the University of Washington, which tested how AI models from Google, OpenAI and Alibaba evaluated English spoken with five accents: American, British, Chinese, Indian and Nigerian.

Across job interviews, conference presentations and English proficiency tests, the models generally ranked American and British speakers highest, Indian speakers in the middle, and Chinese and Nigerian speakers lowest.

The penalty fell mostly on delivery. But content scores for Chinese and Nigerian speakers sometimes slipped, too, even though every speaker read the same script and the models were told to judge only the substance.

“Even though they repeatedly claimed Chinese and Nigerian speakers ‘mumbled’ or were ‘difficult to understand,’ the models were actually very good at transcribing the accented speech,” said Orevaoghene Ahia, a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering and co-lead author of the study.

The stakes go beyond a bad review. Companies increasingly use AI to screen recorded job interviews, and instructors are turning to oral exams as written work gets easier to fake with AI. At least one major English test used for visas and immigration, Pearson’s PTE Academic, relies on AI to score some spoken answers. It was given about 1.2 million times in 2023, according to figures cited in the paper.

The researchers didn’t test the actual products used by hiring platforms or test makers. How those systems work is usually not public, and the paper notes there are no public audits of AI-scored English tests that the authors know of. Instead, the team tested general-purpose models that companies could build on.

“We wanted to check these state-of-the-art models because these are what companies would deploy in a real-world setting,” said Yulia Tsvetkov, a UW associate professor in the Allen School and the study’s senior author.

The research was funded in part by gifts from Google and OpenAI, whose models were among those tested.

To understand the pattern, the researchers measured how acoustically different each accent was from American English. Chinese and Nigerian accents were the farthest away, and models’ scores dropped as that distance grew. Indian and British accents sat close to the American baseline.

The researchers suggest the bias may come from training data that describes accented speakers as unclear, from data sets that underrepresent some accents, or from training that reinforces ideas about how a professional should sound. English is an official language in Nigeria and the language of instruction in Indian schools, yet both accents scored below American and British ones.

The study is the latest in a run of UW research on AI bias. Earlier projects found that AI models favored resumes with white- and male-associated names, that politically slanted chatbots could shift people’s views, and that AI-written children’s stories nearly erased female animal characters.

The team presented the research Oct. 25 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in Budapest. Next, the researchers plan to study more accents, including regional variations within countries, and to look at how AI models handle audio in medical settings such as automated emergency response.

“For all of these, we hope that developers build and publish evaluations of their models that don’t focus only on average performance, but also break it down into subpopulations, dialects and so on,” Tsvetkov said. “We don’t want the average performance to be 97% accurate for the general population, but for a smaller group only 20%.”

#5525. Ring is unveiling an AI-powered home security drone after six years of delays

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Amazon unit launched Ring Robotics with a $1,000 Rover Cam security robot for businesses that is due to ship Dec. 16

Amazon $AMZN's Ring unit introduced Ring Robotics on Tuesday, a line of autonomous security devices that starts with a flying indoor camera called the Ring Drone Cam and a security robot for businesses, the company said.

Ring first announced the drone more than six years before this week's debut, according to Bloomberg. The Drone Cam needs authorization from the Federal Communications Commission before it can be offered for sale or lease, the company said.

The Drone Cam will cost about $250 and ship in late January, according to Bloomberg and Engadget, which gave a Jan. 27 date. TechCrunch listed the price at $270.

The Drone Cam stays docked with its camera off until a flight begins, the company said. Users can set flight routes and schedules, which require a compatible Ring Protect plan, or send it out on demand. When a Ring camera, sensor or alarm is triggered, the drone flies to preset patrol points to investigate. It records 2K video with a 148-degree field of view and uses two built-in LED lights in low light.

Both devices run on a system called AI Pilot, which builds a floor plan as a user carries the drone through a space, suggests patrol points and steers around obstacles, the company said. Aside from getting airborne and touching down, the drone needs artificial intelligence and a working Wi-Fi link to handle almost all of its other functions, according to Bloomberg.

"That kind of invention is hard, and it takes time. But we kept at it until we got it right," Jamie Siminoff, founder and chief inventor of Ring, said in a statement.

Earlier versions struggled with a design problem, according to Bloomberg. Packing in more sensors and computing capability demanded a bulkier battery, and the extra heft called for sturdier rotors that undermined how steadily the drone flew. Siminoff called this "a vicious cycle" at a media briefing, according to Bloomberg. Ring dropped its first design and later shelved a follow-up effort.

The Ring Rover Cam is designed for businesses and patrols on its own, investigates disturbances and streams video in up to 4K, the company said. It has a periscope camera, a siren, a light tower and two-way audio. Ring said the robot was inspired by feedback from customers of Amazon's Astro robot.

The Rover Cam costs $1,000, according to Bloomberg and TechCrunch. It ships Dec. 16, according to TechCrunch.

Recorded video from both devices is protected by an encryption system called Throw Away the Key Encryption, according to Engadget. Ring said both devices have LED indicators that show when they are recording.

#5524. Adobe expands AI assistant into creative workflows

Adobe Inc. today announced an expansion of its CX Enterprise Coworker agentic artificial intelligence platform into its GenStudio content supply chain platform.

The company said the integration move allows creative professionals to bring AI agents into production workflows to develop, manage and deliver personalized marketing content at large scale.

The announcement, made at its Adobe MAX conference in Miami, extends CX Enterprise Coworker beyond its initial focus on customer analytics and marketing into content planning, creation and distribution. The technology provides a conversational interface for coordinating AI agents across Adobe applications and third-party systems.

Adobe said it’s aiming to reduce the manual work involved in producing marketing campaigns while maintaining human oversight and brand consistency. It’s also introducing several new capabilities across its GenStudio portfolio, including AI-assisted campaign planning, automated brand compliance, reusable creative workflows and expanded 3D product visualization.

Central to the initiative is Adobe Brand Intelligence, a machine learning system that captures an organization’s brand standards, including the unwritten practices and preferences that traditionally have resided inside employees’ heads.

“As we move to a world where creatives are directing agents, the context that’s locked in the hearts and minds of creatives is made available to agents so they can start to produce content that is on brand,” said Varun Parmar, Adobe’s senior vice president of GenStudio and Firefly for Enterprise.

Brand Intelligence will be integrated into Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign and Firefly Creative Production for Enterprise. New intelligent asset adaptation capabilities can automatically resize and rearrange campaign designs for different media formats while preserving brand standards.

The system also incorporates continuous learning to keep guidelines current as creative practices evolve.

“It’s ingesting reviews, approvals and rejections by the creatives,” Parmar said. “Based on that information, it’s able to infer the latest guidelines.”

Administrators can inspect and override those conclusions to prevent outdated or incorrect practices from becoming embedded in automated workflows.

Another addition is Ideation Space, a collaborative AI-powered canvas within Adobe Workfront. It combines historical campaign performance, audience information and other enterprise data to help marketers develop campaign briefs.

In a demonstration, Adobe showed how Coworker could retrieve project assignments, research audience characteristics, coordinate with an AI copywriting agent and evaluate proposed designs using synthetic audience simulations. The platform can also be used to run surveys of human respondents.

Adobe is extending Firefly Graph for Enterprise with a feature called Capsules that packages complex creative workflows into simplified applications that other employees can run without mastering the underlying tools. Another feature, Node Publishing, allows teams to share reusable workflow components.

New 3D Digital Twin capabilities enable enterprises to modify product imagery, materials, lighting and camera angles and generate animations without repeatedly photographing physical products.

CX Enterprise Coworker supports external applications and custom-built systems through the Model Context Protocol, enabling enterprises to connect their existing technology investments.

Adobe emphasized that the expansion isn’t intended to give AI agents unrestricted authority over creative decisions. “CX Enterprise Coworker enables human-led agent-accelerated work,” Parmar said. “At every step when the agent is making a decision, it’s coming back to the human and asking.”

Early deployments have accelerated audience definition, traditionally a time-consuming part of campaign development, according to Adobe, although executives provided no quantitative productivity figures. The company expects similar improvements in content production.

The new GenStudio integrations are being made available today, with some Firefly Graph capabilities remaining in beta test. Adobe said the expanded Coworker functionality won’t require additional charges for customers with existing subscriptions.

#5523. Microsoft opens Imagine Cup to startups, and the new rules show how its AI strategy has changed

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 8:04 amNovember 3, 2026 at 8:09 am

Microsoft’s Imagine Cup, a competition for student developers since 2003, is expanding for the first time to early-stage startups whose founders aren’t in school, with $250,000 in cash and $1 million in cloud credits awarded to the winner.

The change, announced Monday, opens the competition to companies founded in the past two years that haven’t raised a Series C round, whether or not their founders are students.

Startups will compete in six industry categories, including cybersecurity, developer tools and healthcare. Students will get a seventh category of their own, with a $25,000 top prize, or they can choose to compete for the main prize in the industry categories.

It’s the latest step in a broader evolution of the Imagine Cup, and the implications go beyond the competition itself. Changes in the rules from 2024 to 2027 show how Microsoft and the tech industry are adjusting, year by year, to the realities of the AI era.

Changing AI requirements: The clearest example is the Imagine Cup rules for AI usage. In 2024, entrants had to build their products with “Microsoft and/or OpenAI” services. In 2025, they had to use at least one Microsoft AI service. In 2026, they had to use at least two Microsoft AI services.

For 2027, they can use any AI they want, as long as they use Microsoft’s Azure cloud.

The shift mirrors a broader change in Microsoft’s AI strategy. The company has added models from Anthropic, xAI, Meta and others to Azure. In April it ended its exclusive cloud arrangement with its longtime AI partner OpenAI, allowing the ChatGPT maker to sell its technology through other platforms such as Amazon Web Services.

Microsoft Foundry, the company’s platform for building AI applications, offers access to more than 11,000 models.

“Imagine Cup 2027 reflects that same approach, giving founders the flexibility to choose the right models and technologies for their solutions while meeting the competition’s Azure and technical requirements,” said Tom Davis, general manager of Microsoft for Startups, in a statement responding to GeekWire’s questions.

Why startups: Addressing the expansion to non-student startups, Davis said AI is letting more founders start companies faster than ever, and the revamped competition is meant to help those young companies win customers and prepare to sell to big businesses.

The judging criteria have changed to match that focus on business customers.

As recently as 2024, student teams couldn’t have raised more than $50,000 in outside funding to compete. Under the new rules, final-round judges, whose scores determine all of the winners, will look for net revenue retention over the previous 12 months, six months of traction data, and a customer reference willing to be contacted.

What’s in it for Microsoft: The change is also a way for Microsoft to bring promising startups onto Azure. For startups in the industry categories, the first-round scoring criteria in 2027 will include “Microsoft and Azure commercial readiness, and expected cloud and AI consumption.”

Azure gets less explicit weight in the final round, whose scores determine the winners. A live production workload on Azure is worth 6 of 100 points there. In 2026, use of Microsoft technology made up 40% of the score in every round.

Participants can also earn Azure credits by using more of Microsoft’s cloud services. The credits start at $1,000 and rise to as much as $150,000 for startups that run at least 10 eligible Azure workloads and spend $3,000 a month on Azure for 60 days.

Amazon and Google run their own credit programs for startups, as the cloud giants compete to win AI companies early, when they’re choosing where to build.

Diversity criteria dropped: The new rules also drop diversity, inclusion and accessibility from the judging criteria, where they had been through 2026. In 2024, inclusion was worth 10% of the score, with judges asked to consider factors such as gender, ethnicity and disability.

Davis said Microsoft “updated the judging framework to reflect the range of industries and customer challenges represented in the competition,” and that inclusion and accessibility remain central to the company’s mission. He added that the competition welcomes startups developing products focused on inclusion and accessibility.

Separately, Microsoft skipped its annual diversity report last year, ending a tradition it started in 2019, as Google, Meta, Amazon and other big tech companies scaled back diversity programs under pressure from the Trump administration.

Prizes and timing: Applications are due Feb. 28. The second-place startup will receive $50,000 and $350,000 in credits, and third place gets $25,000 and $350,000 in credits. The 2026 champion, CopyFlag, a U.K. startup that tracks copies of creators’ designs online, won $150,000.

The top startup in the student category will present at the World Championship but isn’t eligible for the top three prizes, according to the official rules. To compete for those top prizes, student startups can enter an industry category instead, going up against companies that may have raised as much as a Series B.

The rules also allow Microsoft to use “automated assistance” to triage, summarize and compare entries, with human review in advancement decisions.

Winners will be selected in April and announced in May or June at a World Championship, with the date and location still to be determined, Davis said. The 2026 finale was at Microsoft’s Build developer conference in San Francisco.
