#5468. Google launches Gemini for Healthcare, and hospitals like Northwell hope it brings down your medical bill

Google Cloud says its newest AI product can help with one of Americans’ biggest complaints: the cost and redundancies of health care.

On Tuesday, the company launched Gemini for Healthcare, an AI product that connects to the records, billing and insurance systems that hospitals and insurers already use—and is able to act between those systems. Launch customers include Northwell Health, Highmark Health, HCA Healthcare, Optum, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts, Hartford HealthCare and Stanford School of Medicine.

The new healthcare AI can pull a patient’s records from Epic and other systems into one single summary, flag gaps or conflicts between records, prepare and review prior authorizations, check what a patient’s insurance covers, estimate what they’ll owe, and search medical guidelines from groups like ASCO and the BMJ.

This comes as health costs keep climbing. Workers with employer coverage now pay $7,471 a year on average toward family premiums, up 9% from 2025, according to KFF’s annual employer survey released in October. When including what employers contribute, total family premiums rose 5% to $28,303, outpacing a 3.7% rise in wages and 2.7% inflation.

For the head of New York’s largest health system, part of that bill comes from records that don’t talk to each other.

“All the fragmentation of information in healthcare is what has led to, in my mind, some of the costs that have gotten away from us, and also overutilization,” John D’Angelo, who took over as CEO of Northwell in October 2025, told Fortune.

An emergency physician by training, he said he saw it in the ER. “I would treat people de novo, and the information is out there somewhere,” he said. “So I’m either playing detective or I just have to assume.” That could mean ordering a CT scan, he said, not knowing if they’ve had it four times already for the same condition.

When you walk into a doctor’s office, you inevitably are given a clipboard with papers you’re all but certain you’ve completed through the portal online. Then when you finally are whisked away to the doctor’s office, you’re asked the same questions you’re fairly certain were asked in the papers lining that very clipboard.

That constant asking and re-asking of questions leaves a poor taste in patients’ mouths, and that’s all before they were told to go “aaah.” Gemini for Healthcare is solving for that: it cites the source for each finding so clinicians can check it. For now, it can read patient records but not change them, so a doctor or nurse still makes any updates and decisions. In essence, it cuts down on the paperwork a doctor has to complete when they see a patient, bringing back that face-to-face consultation rather than letting paperwork pull doctors away from patients.

“Right now, for every 10 minutes a doctor spends with a patient, they’re 20 minutes on the computer documenting, capturing stuff, looking up the old data, tracking things down,” D’Angelo said.

Much of that time goes to insurers. Prior authorizations, the approvals insurers require before some treatments, are among the biggest burdens. Each physician completes about 40 prior authorizations a week, which takes around 13 hours of physician and staff time weekly, and 40% of practices have staff whose sole job is handling these requirements, according to the American Medical Association. The American Hospital Association estimates administrative costs make up 25% to 35% of U.S. health spending.

At Northwell, the fight with insurers takes a whole department. “I have like 400 employees whose sole job is fighting the insurance denials, and we overturn over 90% of them, but that’s a big labor cost,” D’Angelo said.

Karen Hanlon, president of Highmark Health, which owns both an insurer and the Allegheny Health Network hospitals, said doctors made clear what bothered them most. When Highmark asked its clinicians a few years ago what to fix after prior authorization, she said, “universally they said nothing else. Just keep focusing on prior authorization.”

Aashima Gupta, Google Cloud’s global director of healthcare strategy, said nurses and doctors now spend much of their day moving information between systems. “Humans are acting as an integration layer today,” she told Fortune. “They didn’t get into the profession to be glorified data-entry clerks. They want to be able to take care of the patients.”

Gemini for Healthcare launches with five ready-made “skills” — preset instructions for tasks like summarizing medical records, preparing for appointments and checking a patient’s insurance benefits — plus connectors to Epic, federal Medicare coverage data and medical guidelines from the American Society of Clinical Oncology and the BMJ.

In a demo with Fortune, Will Rosenfeld, Google Cloud’s healthcare data and AI lead, asked the system what was new in an outside specialist’s report that wasn’t in a patient’s Epic chart. In 35 seconds, it pulled the patient’s conditions, medications, allergies and labs, compared them with the outside report and flagged new lab results and an allergy the chart had missed, with each finding linked to its source. A clinician then decides whether to update the chart, since the system can read Epic records but not change them.

“A lot of the power of the product is just like simply one plus one equals three,” Rosenfeld told Fortune, describing how it puts a patient’s record next to coverage rules or medical research.

The same tool can answer cost questions during a visit. Gupta described a nurse asking whether a Medicare patient’s coverage pays for a skilled nursing facility, and what the copay would be, without making calls to find out. Rosenfeld said customers are especially interested in cost estimates. “It’s just something that’s really difficult for patients, to not know what their costs are going to look like,” he said.

Highmark already uses automation to cut waits. It says 78% of approved outpatient prior authorizations submitted digitally now go through automatically, so a patient can sometimes get approval before leaving the office. “They don’t have to take another day off work,” Hanlon told Fortune. She said a clinician reviews every case before Highmark issues a denial.

D’Angelo called automating the denial fights “part of driving the affordability conversation the right way,” and said Northwell runs on “a 1% margin business at best.” Money saved on paperwork, he said, could go to community health workers who keep patients out of the hospital.

He said faster records and notes could also shorten wait times without overworking doctors, letting offices “squeeze two more patients a day” in practices with long waits. “Not because I made them stay open later or I told the doctor, ‘Suck it up, miss lunch,’ but because they’re able to be more efficient,” he said.

“It shouldn’t replace the doctor or the nurse, but it should give the doctor or the nurse back to the patient,” he said.

Both D’Angelo and Hanlon said the potential savings come from catching illnesses earlier, with Gemini acting as a pseudo-preventative care measure, while also allowing people to gain trust within their medical professionals.

D’Angelo, for example, described a system that notices a former smoker turning 50, confirms insurance has approved lung cancer screening, and offers nearby appointments, all without having a human pour through the records in the first place.

“That’s how you also address affordability over the long term, as we get much further upstream on wellness and driving down chronic disease,” he said.

Catherina covers markets, the economy, energy, tech, and AI.

#5467. Agility Robotics co-founder on its Nasdaq debut, lessons from Amazon, and the future of work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 5, 2026 at 6:51 pmNovember 5, 2026 at 6:51 pm

Agility Robotics of Salem, Ore., made its Nasdaq debut Thursday as the first publicly traded U.S. company devoted solely to humanoid robots — offering an ambitious vision for how the technology will change work, and a cautious view of how long it will take.

“Maybe we’ll never have faster-than-light travel. Maybe we’ll never have transporters from Star Trek,” said Jonathan Hurst, the company’s co-founder and chief robot officer. “But we absolutely will have machines that can do all of the physical work that a person can do.”

However, he cautioned, “It’s not going to be next year or five years from now. It’s really a grand challenge.”

Agility went public through a merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC, led by financier Michael Klein. The deal valued Agility at $2.5 billion before the new investment and brought in about $465 million in gross proceeds. Its shares trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT.

After initially dipping below its opening price, the stock closed Thursday at $11.51, up 2.2%, bucking the trend on a day when the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, its worst day in 18 months.

Agility’s robot: The company’s main character is Digit, a two-legged robot with two arms mounted near the top of its torso that let it lift bins high and recover from falls. It moves totes and containers in warehouses and factories.

Digit 5, the latest version, was unveiled in September. Standing 5-foot-11 and weighing 284 pounds, it’s covered in sensors, with cameras and antennas in its head and safety-rated sensors in protective housings around its body. Agility says it can lift 50 pounds, reach 7.2 feet high and work more than 20 hours in a 24-hour day.

But the big advance is that Digit 5 was designed to work alongside people without a barrier. Earlier versions had to be fenced off from workers, which limited where customers could use them.

Agility learned how much that mattered at Amazon, an early investor in the company, which tested prior versions of Digit for moving and stacking bins in its warehouses.

Digit did useful work in tests there, Hurst said, but when Agility asked about scaling up, Amazon said it couldn’t deploy the robots. It showed Agility what it had taken to get its own wheeled robot through three to four years of safety certification, and said it didn’t know how a balancing robot would ever get there.

“The safety case to do this is unbelievably hard,” Hurst said. “Nobody has ever deployed a dynamically stable balancing machine, and it brings new risks.”

Getting a robot out from behind the barrier took years of engineering and standards work. Agility has been co-authoring ISO safety standards for the category and making its case to insurance companies and warehouse operators who want proof in numbers before putting a balancing machine next to a person.

Digit 5 uses AI and multiple sensors to watch for nearby people. Depending on the situation, it steers around them, stops or sits down. Visual and audio cues signal what it’s about to do, and a safety controller triggers its responses when someone gets too close.

Hurst credits the lessons from Amazon, along with ones from GXO, Toyota and Schaeffler, with shaping the design of Digit 5.

“Amazon was a huge, huge part of getting us to that point,” he said.

Amazon made an initial deposit in 2024 toward a $1.05 million purchase of five robots, according to Agility’s filings. Agility recorded about $1.04 million in net sales from Amazon in 2025, 58% of its total for the year. Hurst said he couldn’t speak to whether Amazon is a customer now.

With the safety improvements and other advancements, Hurst called Digit 5 “the scaling moment” for Agility. “That is the unlock,” he said.

One customer, which Agility has not named, has committed to a $300 million, three-year contract for 1,000 Digit 5 robots, according to its filings. The robots would be rented rather than sold, the commitment is subject to milestones and specifications, and the customer gets warrants that vest as the robots are deployed.

Agility has built about 10 Digit 5 robots, Hurst said, with the first prototypes just coming off the line. Its factory in Salem was built to eventually produce as many as 10,000 robots a year.

Financial picture: Agility’s business is still small, with revenue of $1.78 million last year and about $174,000 in the first six months of this year. It lost $362 million in the first half, up from $71.8 million a year earlier. Stock-based compensation, an accounting charge for employee equity awards, rose by about $252 million over the same period.

Agility had $14.7 million in cash at the end of June, before the deal closed, and management said in its interim financial statements that there was substantial doubt about the company’s ability to keep operating.

Hurst called the public markets his biggest unknown.

“I’m completely confident in our market path, our technological path,” he said. If public shareholders agree, he said, Agility will be able to “continue on this mission successfully and raise money when we need to.” If they doubt the company, “that’s going to make our life a lot harder.”

What Agility has that most rivals don’t is robots doing commercial work. As of May, its Digit 4 model had logged more than 65,000 hours across nine committed customer deployments, according to its filings. Digit 4 robots have moved more than 100,000 totes since June 2024 at a Georgia facility run by the logistics company GXO.

Investors have put far higher values on rivals still working largely in pilots, including Figure AI at a reported $39 billion, more than 15 times Agility’s valuation in the merger.

“Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” said Peggy Johnson, Agility’s CEO, in a statement. Going public, she said, gives the company more resources to put Digit into more workplaces.

Johnson became CEO in March 2024, when Hurst moved from CTO to chief robot officer. She previously ran Magic Leap, and before that spent six years as a Microsoft executive, leading business development and dealmaking under CEO Satya Nadella.

In an interview with GeekWire earlier in the week, Hurst took the long view on the stock listing, calling it a milestone on a much longer path. Treating a listing day as the achievement, he said, is a finance person’s frame: “I just don’t live in that world.”

From CMU to OSU: Hurst has been on that path for almost three decades.

He built his first walking robot in 1997, as a freshman at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. He stayed at Carnegie Mellon for a Ph.D. in robotics, finishing in 2008, when fewer than 100 people in the world had earned one, he said.

That year he joined Oregon State University in Corvallis, planning from the start to eventually spin a company out of his research. In his Oregon State lab, Hurst’s team built ATRIAS, a two-legged robot that didn’t look like any animal because it was based on a mathematical model of walking and running. It was the first machine to reproduce the dynamics of human walking.

He started Agility in 2015 with Damion Shelton, a Carnegie Mellon classmate who was CEO until 2024, and Mikhail Jones, one of his Oregon State students, out of his lab there.

Being in Oregon helped from the start, Hurst said. Agility was almost alone in trying to build humanoid robots, and the engineers who moved to Oregon to join it were committed to that mission. The company had almost no turnover, unlike the Silicon Valley pattern of people jumping to a new job every six months.

But as it passed 400 employees, it needed experienced engineering managers, and Oregon had no robotics industry large enough to have produced them. Agility had been hiring those people in California and flying them north, so it opened an office there. Today Agility has offices in Pittsburgh and Fremont, Calif., in addition to Oregon.

Impact on jobs: For the time being, Agility pitches Digit as a way to fill jobs that are difficult to staff. Johnson told TechCrunch this week that the company has focused on “manual, very repetitive jobs, that it’s hard to find humans to do.”

Hurst calls the first commercial uses of the technology “step one” toward what he describes as the dream: “robots as part of everyday human life, doing the things people would rather not do.”

Asked what happens to the people whose work the robots replace, Hurst pointed to farming as an example of automation improving people’s lives.

“Early in American history, 90% of Americans worked in agriculture, and today 2% do,” he said. “And the only reason that’s true is because of automation.”

#5466. It’s Time to Confront the Realities of What Your CRM Can Do — and What It Can’t

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

CRMs can be powerful tools, but they’re not crystal balls.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In the world of franchise recruitment, nothing is more sacred than a quality lead. And at any given time, there are potentially millions of Americans considering an entrepreneurial future, some of whom have always harbored a desire to own and operate a business of their own and others for whom circumstances dictated taking matters into their own hands. Both of these would-be entrepreneurial types are invaluable, as you never know which one may go on to sign an official franchise agreement.

That means tracking every lead is paramount. The majority of franchise sales and development teams are highly reliant on their Customer Relationship Management (CRM) systems to achieve this important task. Thanks to today’s technologies, now fully integrated with the power of AI, CRM databases have become much more complex in both design and functionality. Much thought and consideration go into these factors, providing development teams with what they hope will be an efficient roadmap to meet their outsized recruitment goals.

But there’s a catch. Regardless of how much time, capital and manpower sales and development teams pour into their proprietary CRM systems, they’re not exactly infallible. And that’s where the true issue lies. Accepting this reality means you understand the limitations, making now as good a time as any to confront the reality of what your CRM can do.

Whether you’re starting from scratch or looking to upgrade your CRM’s capabilities, there are some essential factors to consider in finding the right fit for your organization. Ideally, you’re looking to establish a critical technological component of your franchise recruitment effort, a centralized database of candidates that will come to define your “quantity vs. quality” approach.

When assessing your specific needs in a CRM, there are several rhetorical questions involved. But regardless of your organization’s size or its recruitment strategy, your CRM should be designed with long-term value in mind. Here is what’s most important to consider if you want to get started on the right foot:

Once you’ve defined these critical components, your sales and development team is ready to progress to the procurement stage. This is not the time to scrimp on your due diligence, so take the necessary time to evaluate your CRM options and pay close attention to the demos offered by different technology providers.

The very title of this article establishes that CRMs are not the panacea for your franchise recruitment efforts. That’s because, despite the advanced automated capabilities baked into the most technologically advanced CRM, there are still things it cannot accomplish for you. These can be broken down into three key areas:

1. Activity tracking does not guarantee pipeline health

By design, the majority of advanced CRM setups are designed to capture data, manage incoming leads and keep track of real-time updates and activity. And they do a fine job with these capabilities — but what they can’t do is provide your sales and development teams with the predictive analytics necessary to make informed decisions on how to proceed. In other words, it can’t inherently show you the health and viability of your current sales pipeline.

2. Critical datasets may be siloed elsewhere

Even with the most advanced capabilities, including those powered by AI, CRMs can’t truly assess the total investment you’ve made in front-end lead generation and tie that back to long-term backend performance. That’s because the valuable insights you need to make informed decisions may not be readily available in the CRM, but scattered across other networks … even external ones.

In a typical knee-jerk reaction, franchise sales and development teams that miss the mark on their intended recruiting goals immediately go into finger-pointing mode. When signings fall short, the CRM often gets the blame. Before replacing it, examine how your team defines the process, maintains the data and follows through with candidates. But the issue here is franchise development teams mistaking their CRM as a structural sales methodology, when in fact success calls for a more disciplined, human-centric approach.

Franchise recruitment teams can be quick to blame CRM systems when their lead-generation goals go unmet. So, they take the most drastic action first and decide to change it out for something shinier, better and — in almost every instance — more expensive. But even after all those changes, and the requisite amount of time goes by, they find themselves in the exact same situation down the road.

That’s because the standards they’re applying to measure results aren’t where the actual problems lie. More often than not, the real problem is in how they’re utilizing the CRM system and what they’re asking it to accomplish.

By design, CRMs are powerful systems that do an admirable job doing exactly what we program them to do — to the letter. They track activity, manage leads, store critical information for later retrieval, and can provide us with real-time updates of where every candidate is in the process. They keep the pipeline moving smoothly and efficiently. But never mistake that for visibility or predictive analytics.

CRMs are not infallible, and they’re definitely not the crystal ball you’re looking for when it comes to predicting the long-term success of your franchise recruitment goals. Before you blame your CRM, take a hard look at your recruitment process, the quality of your data and who is accountable for moving each candidate forward.

In the world of franchise recruitment, nothing is more sacred than a quality lead. And at any given time, there are potentially millions of Americans considering an entrepreneurial future, some of whom have always harbored a desire to own and operate a business of their own and others for whom circumstances dictated taking matters into their own hands. Both of these would-be entrepreneurial types are invaluable, as you never know which one may go on to sign an official franchise agreement.

That means tracking every lead is paramount. The majority of franchise sales and development teams are highly reliant on their Customer Relationship Management (CRM) systems to achieve this important task. Thanks to today’s technologies, now fully integrated with the power of AI, CRM databases have become much more complex in both design and functionality. Much thought and consideration go into these factors, providing development teams with what they hope will be an efficient roadmap to meet their outsized recruitment goals.

But there’s a catch. Regardless of how much time, capital and manpower sales and development teams pour into their proprietary CRM systems, they’re not exactly infallible. And that’s where the true issue lies. Accepting this reality means you understand the limitations, making now as good a time as any to confront the reality of what your CRM can do.

#5465. Lumen CFO expects up to $1.5 billion from legacy copper amid pivot to AI connectivity

Good morning. As Lumen Technologies transforms from a legacy telecom company into an AI enterprise connectivity provider, it’s finding a new use for its old copper network: mining it.

“Copper is worth more to us mined than operated,” President and CFO Chris Stansbury said.

Lumen plans to turn off copper-based services in Iowa, Florida, Nevada and Utah, about 25% of its copper network, by the end of next year. At current copper prices, Lumen expects $1 billion to $1.5 billion in pretax net proceeds from copper recovery over the next five years, Stansbury said.

The benefits extend beyond the metal. Decommissioning will also cut the operating and capital costs of maintaining aging infrastructure, simplify operations, and free up resources for higher-return investments, he said.

“We’re now at the point in our transformation with legacy where the cash generation from revenue is actually not as good as what will be cash generation from mining the copper that’s in the ground,” Stansbury told me. “This industry is sitting on one of the largest copper mines in the world.”

Lumen plans to work with regulators and meet its service obligations as it stops marketing new copper services.

The strategy is part of a broader effort to reinvent Lumen, No. 354 on the Fortune 500, as an enterprise connectivity provider for the AI era. Lumen pairs its large fiber network with Alkira’s software, which works with any carrier. That lets companies connect and manage their data from one place, whether it sits on Lumen’s network, another provider’s network, in the cloud, or in data centers. The company recently announced three initiatives involving intelligent networking, AI energy challenges, quantum connectivity, and emerging security threats.

There are signs of progress. Lumen reported third-quarter revenue of $2.72 billion, down 12.1% year over year, largely reflecting the sale of its consumer fiber business to AT&T. But adjusted EBITDA reached $715 million, and its adjusted loss of 14 cents per share was narrower than analysts expected.

More importantly, strategic revenue, higher-growth enterprise and fiber-based services, rose 10% to $1.28 billion, driven by AI demand and private connectivity deals. Lumen reaffirmed its full-year EBITDA and free cash flow guidance.

The challenge will be sustaining that growth while replacing the revenue and cash of its legacy business.

CEO Kate Johnson and Stansbury have worked on the transformation for about four years. Johnson envisioned making Lumen’s network easier for businesses to consume.

“What Kate came in, and saw was the ability to effectively cloudify the network, just like the hyperscalers had done with compute and storage,” Stansbury said.

The effort has also required a cultural shift and change management.

“I think the approach that you take in having those conversations and making those tough decisions is treating people with respect and empathy, and being transparent—telling them what you can, when you can,” Stansbury said. He added: “I don’t want to say it makes those decisions easier, but I think it ultimately helps the organization transform from what was to what will be in a much better way.”

Mike Barna was named CFO of Advantive, a provider of software for specialty manufacturing and distribution businesses. Barna brings more than two decades of finance and operating leadership across software and data businesses, most recently as CFO of Lone Wolf Technologies. Consumers are still spending, but they're looking harder for bargains, according to a new Bank of America Institute report. The bank's Spending Tier Composite, a measure built from its card data that tracks whether shoppers are moving between premium, standard and value-tier stores, fell to its lowest level since 2021.

The decline suggests more households are shifting spending to discount stores even as overall spending holds up and consumer confidence stays below pre-pandemic levels. Trading down is strongest in apparel, where tariff-related price increases are reaching shoppers, and in dining. Travel is the exception: the travel measure has risen, but the report says that may be because lower-budget travelers are skipping trips rather than becoming less price-conscious.

Millennials are leading the shift. They've traded down faster than Gen X or Baby Boomers since 2022, particularly in apparel and groceries.

#5464. This Former NASA Engineer Has 85 Million YouTube Subscribers. He Says This Is How to Differentiate Your Videos From AI Slop.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The YouTube star explains what makes content valuable as it gets cheaper to produce.

He rose to fame with YouTube videos like How to Survive a Grenade Blast, which has 100 million views, and Can you swim in Jello?, which has 224 million views.

In a new interview with Business Insider, Rober said the solution to competing against AI slop, or low-quality AI posts, is to go out into the real world and do something noteworthy.

“Do you want to see a simulation of someone dunking a basketball with a sick trick, or do you want to see someone actually do it?” he said. “The fact that you know it’s real is what makes it crazy.”

Rober believes that quality sets his channel apart.

“At least for a while, I think I have a moat on the YouTube channel,” he said. He believes that his real-world experiments and recognizable human personality give his channel an advantage over AI-generated content — at least, for now.

Rober said his YouTube videos generated about $17 million in revenue last year, which is roughly what it cost to produce them. He also makes money through his company CrunchLabs, which sells products like maker kits that introduce young people to science and engineering.

Rober noted that his business now employs more than 200 people. Its mission centers on inspiring curiosity and learning.

“Curiosity is so important in this new age of AI,” Rober said. “It means you just have a lifetime of learning.”

AI introduces a conundrum for content creators. The tools that make videos easier to create are also making it harder for individual channels to stand out. For some creators, AI means more growth. Others say it could cause their work to get lost in the crowd.

One popular use case of AI is to help creators introduce existing videos to audiences who speak different languages. For example, translation startup Linguana builds and manages local YouTube channels with AI dubbing. It includes translated thumbnails and descriptions, providing creators with a way to expand internationally without doing all the translation work themselves.

Services like Linguana can allow creators to generate additional income from content they have already created. In April 2025, Linguana told Business Insider that it was generating 10,000 video translations each month for hundreds of YouTubers. The company takes half the revenue generated through its partnerships rather than charging upfront.

However, easier production ushers in a competitive challenge. Rober said that when more people create similar content, technical execution alone may become less valuable. This means that channels built around anonymous narration or animation could face particular challenges as competitors produce content faster and more cheaply.

He rose to fame with YouTube videos like How to Survive a Grenade Blast, which has 100 million views, and Can you swim in Jello?, which has 224 million views.

#5463. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5462. Let there be LEDs: Tech upgrade helps James Turrell’s Skyspace shine again at UW art museum

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:01 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:42 am

For most of the past dozen years, a James Turrell artwork on the University of Washington campus in Seattle — built to glow at sunrise and sunset — has been running on daylight alone.

That changes Nov. 14, when UW’s Henry Art Gallery relights “Light Reign,” its Turrell Skyspace, after a restoration that replaced aging lights with hundreds of new fixtures and a control system synced to the sun.

Originally installed in 2003 near the Henry’s entrance along 15th Avenue N.E., “Light Reign” is one of dozens of skyspaces by Turrell, the 83-year-old artist known for turning light itself into his medium.

Inside the artwork’s oval chamber, LEDs bathe the walls in slowly shifting color, and when the weather cooperates, a retractable lid opens to an oculus that frames the sky. From outside, the glass-paneled shell lights up with its own program — a 21st-century mood ring just steps from a bronze George Washington who has been gazing west toward the Olympics since 1909.

The relighting comes as the Henry, Washington’s first public art museum, heads into its 100th year. The museum opened on campus in February 1927, and officials are hinting that bigger changes are on the way for the centennial.

Trouble with “Light Reign” started around 2015, said Sage Sommer, the Henry’s director of exhibitions and collections. The original lights, by then more than a decade old, were reaching the end of their lifespan, and over time the museum lost the ability to run them.

Through those years, the Skyspace stayed open. Visitors could still sit inside, meditate and watch clouds and birds pass over the oculus, just without the color.

After years of planning, the Henry settled on a full lighting overhaul that also folds in ideas Turrell has used in his newer skyspaces. The exterior already ran on LEDs, but a very early generation of them, while the interior and oculus were lit by neon tubes made by Western Neon.

The museum didn’t work with Turrell directly. Instead it worked with lighting designer Ryan Pike, whose company, RHMP, works only on Turrell installations, from upgrades of existing pieces to new projects. Pike has worked on Turrell artworks since 2013.

For Pike, the toughest part was the exterior. “It’s just over 700 lights, in nine DMX universes, so each fixture can output independently of the rest,” he said in an email. DMX is the standard protocol for controlling stage and architectural lighting. Splitting the facade across multiple universes lets every fixture be programmed on its own.

Sommer said the Skyspace isn’t strictly time-based media, a museum term for art that relies on equipment and unfolds over time. But it raises the same questions. Sometimes the fix is simple, like converting a VHS tape to a digital file. Other times the hardware is integral to the work. Some artists insist a piece be shown only on a CRT TV, and some come back with a remastered version and want only that one shown.

“We work really closely with the artists to make sure that it is as they envision,” she said.

The Henry isn’t the only museum to face the problem. In 2023, Minneapolis’ Walker Art Center restored its own Turrell skyspace, “Sky Pesher,” after it became impossible to find the cold cathode tubes — a 1920s-era technology — that powered its sunrise and sunset lighting program.

Working with Turrell and his studio, the Walker switched to LEDs, which allowed more control and a much wider range of color. What had been “shades of tinted white” is now multicolored, Joe King, the Walker’s director of collections and exhibition management, said in an interview published by the museum.

The Henry’s new system uses roughly 840 LED fixtures, about 710 outside and 130 inside, Sommer said. The exterior program kicks in a half-hour before dawn and dusk. The morning show is brief, about 36 minutes, while the evening one currently runs about four hours after sunset.

“The very cool thing about this space, because we are so far north, is just how connected to sunrise and sunset it is, and how drastically different it is throughout the year,” Sommer said.

The roof has its own engineering pedigree. The Skyspace’s hydraulic lid, which lifts and slides out of the way, was designed by submarine manufacturers in Everett. It stays shut in the rain.

The museum closed the Skyspace in late July and used the downtime for physical restoration, too: repainting the interior, refinishing the teak benches, waxing floors, replacing worn locks, refitting doors that had swollen and cleaning out the gutters. Everything had to be rewired, and the project took longer than expected.

“Light Reign” is the most visible piece in the Henry’s collection of about 30,000 objects, including more than 18,000 textiles and 7,000 works on paper. Only a sliver is ever on view, so the Henry is putting its collection database online. The project was funded by UW’s Student Technology Fee. Anyone can book an appointment at its study center to see a piece up close.

Technology is also the focus of the Henry’s centennial exhibition, opening in late February. Swagato Chakravorty, associate curator, said he was surprised that no major museum had mounted a large, ambitious show on contemporary art and technology in decades, even as Seattle was transformed around it. His show looks at technology “from below,” focusing on the people and communities most directly affected rather than a “great man” story.

The exhibition is loosely organized around three threads. One is bioethics, including a work the Henry commissioned in 2002 with UW geneticist Mary-Claire King, which is being revived 25 years later. Another pairs Indigenous knowledge with tools like 3D printing and algorithms. The third is technology’s material toll, from data centers to water use.

Chakravorty said he deliberately avoids taking a side on whether technology is good or bad for art.

“Writing is a technology. Cave painting was a technology,” he said. As for AI: “It’s not going to kill art.”

The public unveiling of the refurbished “Light Reign” runs 3:30 to 6 p.m. Nov. 14, with remarks from Henry Executive Director Kris Lewis and the exterior illumination starting at 4 p.m. Admission is free, though the Henry encourages RSVPs, and interior viewing is limited to 25 people at a time for about 10 minutes each.

#5461. Exclusive: In the race for robot training data, ex-Meta researchers’ startup turns to gig workers with cameras

Memories.ai is paying people to show robots how to do their jobs. The San Francisco startup supplies first-person video data for robot training, with cameras capturing the hands-on details of preparing food, stocking shelves and repairing equipment.

The company is launching Memories Upload, a global gig-work platform where contributors take paid video-recording tasks to help train robots. Its wearable LUCI Pin camera, developed by Memories.ai, weighs under 45 grams and attaches magnetically to mounts worn on a person’s head, chest or wrist. It captures POV video of the contributors doing various tasks. Two cameras can be paired for stereo capture, providing views that help estimate depth.

Memories.ai says its network recorded more than 1 million hours of first-person video in the platform’s first month in beta and that it aims to collect more than 10 million hours by March 2027. The company was founded by former Meta researchers Shawn Shen and Ben Zhou. The company has raised $16 million in venture capital funding to date, including an $8 million seed round in July 2025 led by Susa Ventures, with investors including Samsung Next, and an $8 million “seed extension” in June this year.

Humanoid robotics startup Figure and Physical Intelligence, a startup that builds AI software “brains” that can control a variety of different types of robots and embodied AI devices, are both exploring how robots can learn from POV video footage. Figure’s Index platform pays people to record everyday tasks for its Helix AI models. Physical Intelligence has tested combining human video with teleoperation data, which is recorded as people control robots remotely, demonstrating how to complete tasks or handle unfamiliar objects and environments. Physical Intelligence co-founder Sergey Levine wrote in a blog post that human video and other supplementary data could provide “a source of knowledge about what can happen in the real world,” complementing data collected by robots themselves.

For a robot learning to make coffee, those recordings could show how someone grips a cup, positions it beneath a grinder and moves it without spilling. Footage from different kitchens, tools and ways of working can expose models to a wider variety of tasks and environments. Developers still work out how to translate those observed movements into actions suited to the robot’s own body.

“Recognizing an activity is different from understanding exactly how a hand grips a tool, moves an object or completes a step, especially when the camera is moving and objects are partly hidden,” Rick Zhuang, director of product and engineering for Cosmos at Nvidia, which works with Memories.ai, told Fortune.

Finding those details in a growing collection of footage is part of the problem Memories.ai is trying to solve. The company uses Nvidia’s Metropolis Video Search and Summarization tools to optimize video streaming and processing. Its video-captioning model is fine-tuned from Cosmos, Nvidia’s family of models for understanding the physical world, and it also uses Cosmos-based models to label actions. The company further trains Cosmos on curated video for customers’ specific tasks, a process known as post-training.

The resulting descriptions are tied to specific moments, letting developers search for an action and retrieve relevant examples without watching hours of recordings. “What stands out is the focus on making everyday human experience searchable and useful for robot learning,” Zhuang said of Memories.ai.

The company says its customers include three of the top five frontier AI labs, alongside robotics developers buying its first-person training data, although the company declined to name these customers citing non-disclosure agreements. Co-founder and CEO Shawn Shen told Fortune that customers increasingly want footage covering a wider range of work environments, tasks and camera angles. Two people making coffee in different kitchens can supply useful variation, he said, even when they are completing the same task. Developers also request wrist-level footage to see interactions that a camera on someone’s head might miss, such as exactly when a hand touches an object.

Adam Scraba, Nvidia’s head of physical AI ecosystem for vision agents, told Fortune that the wide variety of specialized tasks in heavy industry, coupled with the need for highly accurate models, presents one of the field’s hardest challenges.

“The training dataset for Vision AI and video analysis becomes critically important for basically all Physical AI solutions. Developers need to find the right corner-case examples, trust their labels and trace each annotation to the moment it describes,” he said.

Producing labels developers can trust is particularly difficult when hands make subtle movements, objects are partly hidden or the boundary between two actions is unclear, Zhuang said. Those cases make human review and evaluation essential. Human video is most useful alongside robot demonstrations and simulation, he added, helping developers connect observations of human work to actions a robot can perform.

Update, Nov. 10: This story has been updated to clarify the total amount of money Memories.ai has raised to date and to include information about the company’s June 2026 seed extension round.

Wen Shao is a reporting fellow at Fortune covering AI, with a focus on the companies, economics, and infrastructure shaping the industry.

#5460. Amazon’s AI shopping agent moves into text messages, taking orders and tracking prices

by Todd Bishop on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:07 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:35 am

Amazon is rolling out a new feature to let customers shop by text message — sending requests to its Alexa for Shopping AI agent, which will search for products, compare options and place orders on their behalf.

The idea is to make shopping work more like messaging a personal assistant. Amazon says the agent works in the background after it gets a request or a photo, and texts back when the task is done.

It’s part throwback and part hot new thing, reflecting a broader shift in how tech companies are offering AI agents for everyday use. OpenAI added texting to Dot, its personal AI agent, last month, and DoorDash rolled out text ordering in September.

The expansion of Amazon’s AI shopping assistant comes amid a larger fight over who controls online shopping when agents do the buying. Amazon has moved to block outside agents from Meta, Perplexity, Google and OpenAI from shopping its site while building its own.

The text thread is also a new place for Amazon to sell. The company says order updates, delivery notifications and deals will eventually land in the same conversation.

Digiday reports that sponsored products can appear among the options the agent texts back, free to advertisers for now, while purchases the agent completes on its own stay ad-free. Amazon reported $68.6 billion in advertising sales in 2025.

The text feature started rolling out Friday to a small group of U.S. customers by invitation, and millions more will get access in the coming weeks, the company says.

Customers who opt in get a contact called “Alexa Shopping” and can send it requests that range from a note that they’re out of dog food to a photo of a recipe they want turned into a grocery order, according to Amazon’s examples.

The agent searches, texts back with options and completes the purchase with the customer’s approval. Customers can also turn on auto-buy to have it purchase an item automatically when the price hits their target. It can also watch for price drops, reorder past purchases and check on packages, and Amazon says a conversation started by text will carry over to the Amazon app, the website and Alexa devices.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, merging its Rufus shopping chatbot with Alexa+, the generative AI version of its voice assistant.

#5459. Alta raises $48 million for its compliance-focused blockchain in Series A round led by Index Ventures

Financial firms looking to accelerate money transfers with crypto have no shortage of options when it comes to blockchains, including Ethereum, Solana and Avalanche. That hasn’t deterred a startup called Alta from trying to lure banks and big companies with a blockchain of its own. The chain seeks to stand out with its plug-and-play compliance layer that lets customers ensure that any transactions they process are consistent with rules and regulations anywhere in the world.

On Tuesday, Alta announced it has raised a $47.5 million a Series A round at an undisclosed valuation. The new round, which was led by Index Ventures, comes after the startup raised $32.5 million in seed funding backed primarily by the Australian fintech giant Airwallex, which is taking on Stripe and others in the global payments space.

The CEO of Alta is Loong Wang, who founded an earlier crypto startup that he sold in 2021, and then pivoted to a second startup that employs quantum computing to aid in drug discovery. Wang returned to crypto technology to found Alta, which recently rebranded from its original name of Metal, alongside former Meta executive Catherine Porter, who helped oversee the company’s since-abandoned crypto venture.

“We often say we wouldn’t have built an L-1 if we didn’t have to,” said Wang, noting that Alta’s features include one that prevents random people from sending funds to those with an address on the blockchain. (Most blockchains allow for so-called “airdrops” that oblige wallet holders to accept funds whether they want to or not).

Alta, which has 25 employees and offices in San Francisco and Melbourne, is also notable for its close ties to Airwallex. Those ties include a personal connection between Wang and Airwallex CEO Jack Zhang, who was a crypto skeptic, but recently acknowledged the inherent value of stablecoins when it comes to cheap and efficient money transfers.

Airwallex is also serving as a massive distribution channel for Alta, persuading its global network of customers to use the startup’s platform for crypto transactions. This comes at a time when Airwallex’s main rivals, including Stripe and its Tempo blockchain, are likewise building out crypto infrastructure.

“With the rise of agentic banking and programmable payments, stablecoins are becoming an important vector for settlement,” said Zhang in a statement announcing Alta’s latest funding round.

Also participating in the Series A funding round were GV (Google Ventures), Blackbird Ventures, Square Peg and Capital49, a venture firm established by Airwallex’s cofounders.

Jeff John Roberts is the Finance and Crypto editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of the blockchain and how technology is changing finance.

#5458. Ripple Insider Sold 2.5M XRP, But Still Thinks Its Price Could Flip Bitcoin

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

David Schwartz sold 2.5 million XRP in 2025, but the Ripple veteran isn’t giving up on the coin at this price. The former CTO recently revealed a $1.7 million capital gains tax bill while defending himself against accusations of dumping. His latest comments also revived an ambitious XRP Price debate about whether the token could eventually overtake Bitcoin.

The $1.7 million I paid in capital gains tax says otherwise.

Schwartz confirmed the sale after critics questioned his commitment to XRP. He said nearly all the tokens came from bonuses received for his work in 2020 and 2023. Rather than quietly dismissing the accusations, he shared evidence of the taxes paid on those transactions.

But selling millions of tokens hasn’t stopped Schwartz from entertaining an even stronger possibility. During an X Spaces discussion, he agreed that XRP could eventually surpass Bitcoin in market cap.

Schwartz’s selling history stretches much further back than the 2025 transactions. The XRP Ledger co-creator previously revealed that his holdings peaked at 26 million XRP.

By August 2026, that balance had fallen to around 2 million tokens. He acknowledged selling most of his holdings, although some also went toward gifts and transfers. That represents a substantial reduction from his previous position.

His earliest sales began when XRP traded around $0.10. Schwartz admitted he never expected the coin to break $0.25. He also regretted selling 40,000 ETH for just $1.05 apiece.

The developer explained that he dislikes taking excessive financial risks. He and his wife followed a strategy of selling portions whenever their investments reached new all-time highs. The approach helped them reduce exposure and sleep better at night.

That strategy explains why Schwartz could sell millions of XRP without necessarily abandoning its long-term potential. He has also disclosed that much of his remaining financial exposure shifted toward Ripple equity.

His September comments offer another important clue about his conviction. Asked whether XRP could eventually overtake Bitcoin, Schwartz answered affirmatively. He clarified that XRP would need to grow faster rather than Bitcoin necessarily losing value.

He described the outcome as probably more likely than not, although he offered no timeline. Schwartz also stopped short of providing a specific XRP Price target.

For perspective, September’s market-cap comparison put XRP near $90 billion and Bitcoin around $1.57 trillion. XRP would have needed approximately $25 to match Bitcoin’s valuation at those market levels. That calculation is illustrative.

Bitcoin’s position as crypto’s leading asset comes from something deeper than its market capitalization. Satoshi Nakamoto introduced Bitcoin in October 2008 as a peer-to-peer electronic cash system.

The original whitepaper challenged the need for financial institutions to control digital payments. Banks and central authorities had become trusted intermediaries, despite their ability to freeze accounts and influence monetary supply.

Bitcoin offered a different arrangement through cryptographic verification and a distributed network. Its creator even embedded a newspaper headline about bank bailouts into the January 2009 genesis block.

That message remains central to Bitcoin’s appeal. Investors increasingly view BTC as an alternative to traditional monetary systems, where governments can expand money supplies and financial institutions control access.

XRP approaches the problem differently. The XRP Ledger uses a validator-based consensus mechanism, while Ripple remains a major commercial force behind its ecosystem. Its payment infrastructure prioritizes transaction speed and institutional settlement.

Bitcoin’s permissionless monetary foundation offers a different proposition. This gap also explains interest in projects attempting to expand Bitcoin’s functionality without replacing its underlying network.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is developing a Bitcoin Layer 2 using the Solana Virtual Machine. Its proposed architecture combines faster transactions, decentralized applications, staking, and DeFi functionality with settlement commitments to Bitcoin’s Layer 1.

The project is a bridge that verifies Bitcoin block headers and transaction proofs before representing BTC on its Layer 2. It also plans to use zero-knowledge proofs to validate transactions and periodically commit network state to Bitcoin.

The presale has recently raised more than $33.2 million raised, with a token price of $0.0136 and staking rewards of 35%. Its development updates also identify November 26 as an important milestone, giving prospective participants a limited window before the next announced stage.

That timeline adds urgency to the developing Bitcoin Layer 2 narrative. Comparing XRP with Bitcoin-based alternatives, the gap is increasingly important. XRP offers an established payments network, while Bitcoin represents a monetary system designed around independence from centralized financial intermediaries.

Schwartz may have sold millions of XRP to reduce personal risk. Yet his willingness to entertain a future where XRP overtakes Bitcoin shows that he hasn’t dismissed its potential.

Whether that vision becomes reality will depend on adoption, liquidity, and actual network usage. For now, the XRP Price debate has another unlikely participant: one of the people who helped build the ledger.

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 6, 2026 at 10:06 amNovember 6, 2026 at 10:45 am

— Amitabha “Guppy” Gupta, a Fred Hutch Cancer Center associate director who helps researchers translate their work to broader audiences, is leaving after 14 years to join Amazon. Starting Nov. 16, he will be a strategic advisor for nonprofit research and advanced AI with AWS’ Global Nonprofit Business.

Gupta said technology was often an obstacle to scientific breakthroughs at Fred Hutch.

Reuters notes that her seven years serving on the Microsoft board “are her closest brush with the tech sector” prior to taking the top job at the PC maker.

At IonQ, the theoretical quantum mechanics expert built MindRoom, an open-source collaboration and knowledge-sharing platform that he calls “a company brain.”

“With this new opportunity, I get to keep building and turbocharging MindRoom with a team of people who are just as excited about AI as I am,” Nijholt said, adding that the tool will remain freely available.

Augmodo ranks No. 122 on the GeekWire 200.

Because the carbon intensity of grid power varies throughout the day and across regions, Neuralwatt’s technology can help customers run compute-intensive operations when clean energy is more abundant.

Lau has been with the telecom giant for 22 years over two stints and serves as VP of digital experience engineering. He holds bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees in electrical engineering from the UW.

— Christian Smith, an Issaquah, Wash.-based tech leader, has been named president of revenue for Cloudflare, which provides security and speed services for websites and online applications. He will oversee worldwide go-to-market operations. Smith previously served as chief revenue officer for Splunk and Nintex.

#5456. Meet the 27-year-old former firefighter who left Goldman to build a used-truck marketplace that’s now valued at $225 million

Martin Hunt joined the volunteer fire service at 15 in his corner of northern Delaware, just outside Philadelphia. Along with fighting fires, he eventually took on a less glamorous part of keeping a department running: selling its old trucks.

It was a lot harder than it sounds. A department that buys a new engine often needs to sell the one it replaced to help pay for it. However, finding a buyer meant cold-calling departments across the country or sending the truck to a local auction, where a vehicle that another town could use might unfortunately go for scrap.

Last year, the very same engine that carried Hunt to his first fire went up for sale. His hometown department’s board hoped to get $30,000. Instead, it sold within days for $125,000, Hunt said, on the online marketplace he had built with his cofounder, Alaz Sengul.

Their company, Garage, is building a nationwide marketplace for the trucks that keep communities running. It connects departments ready to sell with buyers who can’t afford new equipment or wait years for it to arrive, because a truck one town has replaced can still have a long working life somewhere else.

Now the 27-year-old former firefighter, who later worked in private equity at Goldman Sachs, has raised $41 million to grow it. The Series B, led by Invus Opportunities, values the startup at $225 million and brings its total funding to $60 million, the company told Fortune.

By 2023, Hunt was a private equity investor at Goldman Sachs when a friend from his old fire department reached out. The friend had taken over Hunt’s equipment duties and wanted to know how Hunt had managed to make it look so easy.

“I told him it wasn’t easy. I just didn’t complain a ton,” Hunt said.

Not much had changed since Hunt did the job nearly a decade earlier. Departments still leaned on auctions and word of mouth, and new trucks had only gotten harder to come by. Instead, Hunt said new truck can cost millions of dollars and take years to arrive.

The call got Hunt and Sengul, whom he met through a mutual friend at Columbia University, thinking about whether those sales could move online. Sengul had worked as a software engineer at Twitter (now X) and later at the AI note-taking startup Mem, while Hunt knew firsthand what the departments they hoped to serve were up against.

So they quit their jobs with no funding and no product, living off their savings as they built Garage. After joining Y Combinator’s winter 2024 batch, they moved to San Francisco and launched the marketplace early that year.

Garage doesn’t own the trucks, and there’s no lot full of fire engines waiting for buyers. Vehicles stay with their sellers until someone buys them, then go straight to their new home, which is often a long drive away. More than 90% of transactions cross state lines, Hunt said, and the average piece of equipment travels 1,400 miles.

Moving an 80,000-pound truck across the country takes more than a “buy now” button. Garage uses AI tools that appraise equipment and coordinate freight, and buyers anywhere in the lower 48 states can punch in a ZIP code for an instant delivery quote. The company also offers financing and optional warranties.

Hunt compares it to adding a T-shirt to your Amazon cart: buyers know the price, the shipping cost, and when it will show up. The goal, he said, is “an experience that feels a lot more like an Amazon than a Craigslist,” even when the item in the cart weighs tens of thousands of pounds and costs hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Still, a fire truck isn’t a T-shirt. Buyers can trade inspection reports with sellers and book video walkarounds, but buying anything used carries risk. “At the end of the day, they’re buying a used trash truck or a used fire truck, and so things do go wrong,” Hunt said.

Garage says it serves more than 1,000 communities across all 50 states and Canada. Hunt said equipment sales through the platform top $100 million on an annualized basis. The company makes money by charging sellers a 10% success fee on buy-now purchases and buyers a 10% premium at auction. Garage did not disclose its revenue.

For sellers, a bigger pool of buyers can mean real money. South Charleston, West Virginia, budgeted a few hundred thousand dollars from surplus sales in 2025 and instead brought in $1.2 million through Garage, Hunt said. The windfall helped pay for replacement equipment and firefighter cancer screenings.

“An extra million dollars has a real impact on a community,” Hunt said in a statement to Fortune. “Those funds can be reinvested in schools, roads, and local employees without increasing the burden on taxpayers.”

Burlington, Vermont, had previously sold surplus fire equipment through local auctions, often with little to show for it, Fire Chief Michael LaChance said in a testimonial on Garage’s website.

“Basically, we’d take what we could get, which wasn’t much,” he said.

After using Garage, LaChance said, “We got about five times more for our equipment selling with Garage than we did on our own.” According to the company, the proceeds will help replace the department’s command vehicle.

The new funding will go toward hiring and expanding into public works and sanitation. Fire trucks, it turns out, aren’t the only rigs looking for a second life; private sanitation companies are already Garage’s fastest-growing customer segment, Hunt said.

Even in fire, where Garage calls itself the largest source of used trucks in the country, Hunt estimates the company works with about 1% of the market.

“Even in our largest categories, we have a long way to go,” Hunt said.

#5455. How to be unemployed: Glenn Kelman on life after Redfin

by Glenn Kelman on Nov 6, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 12:52 pm

After 20 years at Redfin, and 10 months of unemployment, I’ve co-founded a new company. My business partner and I will announce our plans after we’ve built our product, but in the meantime GeekWire asked me to explain what I learned in the transition between Redfin and this new venture.

Many of us are in transition because society is in transition, with AI hollowing out big companies and making it easier to start new companies.

In the past, my own transitions had been harrowing, because I ran out of money or lost my sense of purpose. Leaving Redfin, I thought “here we go again.” I felt self-conscious being in the grocery store at 11 a.m. on a weekday. I was ashamed when I couldn’t come up with an idea for a company. But I made it to the other side.

To do that, I had to convince myself that I was an intrepid explorer, even if what I was exploring wasn’t Mount Everest, but instead what I could be. I wanted to feel brave about encounters I otherwise would’ve found embarrassing. Over the last year, I met people about becoming a high school teacher, a Whistler bagel shopkeeper, a candidate for the state legislature, the founder of a tree-planting nonprofit, the CEO of a pre-IPO company and a project leader for Sound Transit.

The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.

At the beginning of my exploration, a CEO recruiter told me the startup scene in Seattle was “dead” and that, for all of Seattle’s talent, more companies were forming in New York and even LA. I Googled “high-growth Seattle startups” and the list included one company that went bankrupt in 2023, and Redfin, which was acquired in 2025.

Another friend told me that she was on a Discord channel with a bunch of CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at businesses with legacy codebases. At least for me, the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.

“The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.”

It took me months to feel ready to do that. In January, a friend told me I wasn’t allowed to make any big decisions until September. Another said I had to wait until the frenzy of my last job had subsided. “You’ll know it has happened,” he said, “because food will start tasting better” (it never happened).

At a conference, a fashion entrepreneur who’d built and abandoned vast residences in Jackson Hole and Costa Rica, and got divorced twice in the past three years, gave me a bracelet that said “we are enough.”

Since I’d often been thinking I hadn’t done enough in the morning to deserve lunch, it was a relief to feel that I didn’t have to be creative or productive in order to justify my existence. But relieving that pressure also made it easier to be creative and productive.

On a call walking through Volunteer Park, I told a friend that the bracelet reminded me I could be happy and never start a company again. She said, “YOU JUST NEED A CO-FOUNDER.”

She told me to share flawed ideas with people who could make them better. I set up meetings with potential co-founders, and we shared our ideas before they were ready, because our meetings had become deadlines. Then we used AI to turn our ideas into products, so we could see what was good and bad about each idea. Starting a company started to feel like a natural progression, instead of Athena sprouting out of Zeus’s head.

When I confessed to a friend that everything we were working on still seemed so small, she said, “What about breakfast burritos?” She outlined her vision for a shop serving breakfast burritos all day, with a line out the door. Then she started talking about inventing a nursing home “that makes everyone happy.” Rather than running a McKinsey market-sizing analysis, she just thought about what she wanted to exist in the world.

That’s something almost anyone can do. In her living room, I suddenly felt that humanity would always have an instinct — this is a bizarre word, but it’s what popped into my head — to fructify. I remember walking home from her house with my wife and hearing the thick sound of insects humming in the night as proof of life’s rich pageant. This is what I mean by surrounding yourself with good vibes.

The last step in my process maybe should’ve come first, choosing where I wanted to make a difference. I thought about all the companies that I honestly would’ve been proud to start, and they were all in the same industry. I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing. I met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea, and a business partner who helped me think it through.

Through all of this, I depended on my wife more than any husband ever should. She works herself to the bone treating people with cancer, but she took my calls in the middle of her workday, when I would talk in detail about what to cook for dinner and then — one more thing! — what’s the meaning of my life?

Once, she was getting into our Chevy Bolt for her morning commute while I was rounding the corner with the dog, and I saw her brighten in the way many people did back when I was Redfin’s CEO.

I found myself full of anticipation. She reached into the car, as if to grab a small gift, and heaved something at me from across the street, saying it “needs reprogramming.” Before I realized it was a garage clicker, I thought she had said I was the one who needed reprogramming. “Maybe that’s true,” I said to myself, trudging past the browned lawn, and the dirty dishes, and into a world of possibilities.

#5454. After a summer of reorganizing national debt, the Treasury borrowed more than $100 billion a week in October

The fiscal year of 2027 is not off to a great start for the U.S. Treasury’s pocket book.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) just released its October budget report, the first month of the 2027 fiscal calendar year.

The strictly nonpartisan CBO reported that in October 2026, it estimated the federal government incurred a deficit of $409 billion—more than $100 billion a week. This is $125 billion more than the shortfall recorded last October.

Revenues were $36 billion lower, and outlays were $89 billion higher than the same month last year, according to the CBO. The report suggested October’s federal deficit was that much higher due to shifts in the timing of certain federal payments that otherwise would have been made on November 1 (that date fell on a weekend in 2025 and 2026, therefore pushing those payments into October of each year).

This comes after a summer of debt reshuffling in the U.S. Treasury, with fiscal hawks questioning whether Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was moving deckchairs on the Titanic, rather than meaningfully improving the macroeconomic picture.

Bessent described this summer’s actions as a “Treasury twist,” a reference to policymaker action in which longer-dated Treasuries are bought and paid for by issuing shorter-term debt. The strategy has not been confirmed verbatim by the Treasury, but Bessent himself has indicated the scheme worked by buying back more expensive, long-term debt (in which yields, and hence interest, are higher) in lieu of cheaper, short-term debt.

The move did not impress markets. JPMorgan’s co-head of global fundamental research, James Sullivan, described it as “paying your mortgage with your credit card. It can work for a while, but eventually the mismatch starts to become more obvious.”

Context has since achieved the desired effect: A range of factors (including tough Fed talk on inflation and the recent AI rout) have brought down longer-dated yields and smoothed volatility.

While this has made government borrowing relatively cheaper in the long term (interest rates are tied to long-dated Treasury yields), it will do little to reassure debt hawks the U.S. fiscal trajectory is on a sustainable path.

In its budget review, the CBO showed that for the fiscal year of 2026, the deficit was at 6.2% of the nation’s GDP, up from 5.8% a year prior. This percentage is greater than the 50-year average of 3.8%, and has only previously been matched or exceeded eight times since 1946: from 2009 through 2012 and in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024.

The total deficit for the year was $1.9 trillion, the CBO added, with $1.14 trillion spent on interest on the public debt.

Government income was up for the year to $5.4 trillion, up $169 billion in the 2025 fiscal year, thanks, in large part, to increases in collections of individual income and payroll taxes. But, on the contrary, total outlays increased by $217 billion—most of which came from an uptick in Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid.

Eleanor Pringle is an award-winning senior reporter at Fortune covering news, the economy, and personal finance. Eleanor previously worked as a business correspondent and news editor in regional news in the U.K. She completed her journalism training with the Press Association after earning a degree from the University of East Anglia.
